GeoScope: Training-Free Program Execution beyond the Counting Horizon for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Question Answering

Journal: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
Guohui Deng Email: dlyj0207@whu.edu.cn Corresponding author: Corresponding author. Note: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: School of Internet, Anhui University, Hefei, 230039, China Affiliation: National Engineering Research Center for Agro-Ecological Big Data Analysis & Application, Anhui University, Hefei, 230601, China    Yuhang Jiang Note: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: School of Internet, Anhui University, Hefei, 230039, China    Chengjun Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Cyberspace Security, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, 411105, China    Zhongwen Hu Affiliation: School of Architecture and Urban Planning, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, 518060, China    Zhaocong Wu Affiliation: School of Remote Sensing and Information Engineering, Wuhan University, Wuhan, 430079, China    Linsheng Huang Affiliation: School of Internet, Anhui University, Hefei, 230039, China    Jinling Zhao Affiliation: School of Internet, Anhui University, Hefei, 230039, China    Chao Ruan Affiliation: School of Internet, Anhui University, Hefei, 230039, China    Miaozhong Xu Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Information Engineering in Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing, Wuhan University, Wuhan, 430079, China    Chi Chen Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Information Engineering in Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing, Wuhan University, Wuhan, 430079, China
Abstract

In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision–language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of the former from splitting. On MME-RealWorld counting it gains 11.4 points, and we show that an option that is almost never correct yet often chosen distorts comparisons there. Project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoScope/.

Keywords: 
Remote sensing visual question answering , Ultra-high-resolution imagery , Vision–language model , Object counting , Spatial program , Training-free

1 Introduction

††footnotetext: Abbreviations: MME-RS, the remote sensing part of MME-RealWorld; OSR, object spatial relationship; RC, regional counting; UHR, ultra-high resolution; VLM, vision–language model; VQA, visual question answering.

Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, with scenes of several thousand to ten thousand pixels on a side, have become a standard test of whether vision–language models (VLMs) can support Earth observation (Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025b; Ni et al., 2026). Many of their questions concern small objects in large places, such as how many trucks are parked in the lot below the white building, or in which direction a pool lies from the tennis court. The same questions arise in practice. Inventories of vehicles, ships or storage tanks, damage counts after a disaster and the layout of facilities for planning all depend on how many objects a place holds or where one lies relative to another. A VLM sees a few million pixels per image, so a scene of ten thousand pixels is shrunk at least fivefold per side, and a car that spans 15 pixels at a ground sampling distance of 0.3 m keeps two or three. Before any object is recognised, a method must therefore decide which part of the scene the model sees and at what resolution.

Existing methods address where to look. Trained UHR models extend the visual context, adapt to the ground sampling distance or learn where to zoom through fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or self-distillation (Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026c; Zhu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Dang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026a). Training-free methods keep the model frozen and choose its input instead, by searching over zoom levels (Shen et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025), retrieving patches (Wang et al., 2025e), following attention (Liu et al., 2026d), selecting evidence (Ma et al., 2026b) or directing gaze (Zhang et al., 2026c). Both lines assume that once the right view is chosen, the counts and directions the VLM gives in it can be trusted. For counting this does not hold. Of position, colour and counting, the three MME-RealWorld remote sensing categories, counting is the weakest for every method that reports all three (Section 6.2). WeaveEarth notes that it “is still prone to errors on counting tasks” (Ma et al., 2026b), and question-guided gaze raises MME-RealWorld counting accuracy by less than half a point, from 21.35% to 21.78% (Zhang et al., 2026c). Besides where to look, UHR question answering therefore has to ask when the VLM’s observations can be trusted.

We answer this question as one calibrates a sensor. On DOTA aerial images with exact counts, Qwen3-VL-8B counts up to about five objects in a single view with little bias (Fig. 1). Beyond that its answers fall increasingly short and often settle on round numbers, like a sensor saturating beyond its dynamic range. We call the range of reliable counts the counting horizon. All eight open VLMs we test, from three families, saturate in the same way, most of them beyond about five objects (Section 3.1). The horizon narrows as the view grows and its objects appear smaller. In small views shown magnified, Qwen3-VL-8B counts up to 160 objects to within 21%, but in large views at native resolution it falls short at every number of objects. On cars in FAIR1M and ships in DIOR, two aerial datasets with smaller images, the horizon lies further out.

Beyond the horizon, the natural remedy is a smaller unit of observation, that is, a split view. Splitting recovers much of the shortfall, yet most objects still end in parts that hold more than five, and an empty part is answered with one or two spurious objects on average. An empirical power-law model of the VLM’s counts, the response curve of this sensor, predicts from unsplit views alone how much of the shortfall each split recovers (Section 3.2). The prediction holds on a second, independently drawn set of crops and, mostly within 20%, for seven other models. Its spurious-count term also explains the problem of fixed grids: a grid fine enough for crowded regions overcounts sparse ones. The result is a single rule, to split a view only when its count exceeds the counting horizon. The response model does not run inside the method. Like a calibration, it supports the rule, and at run time the method needs only one threshold, the horizon.

Directions show a similar limit. In the direction questions of UHR-Micro the two objects are already marked with rectangles, and their boxes alone determine the answer, yet Qwen3-VL-8B answers only about two thirds of them correctly (Section 6.3). Even when the objects are marked and visible, the VLM’s judgement of their relative direction cannot be relied on.

Building on these measurements, we present GeoScope (Fig. 2), which treats the VLM as a sensor with a calibrated operating range. The VLM only grounds objects and counts locally within that range, while the spatial reasoning, from delimiting regions and summing the counts of split views to judging directions, is done by deterministic geometric operations. To our knowledge, GeoScope is the first UHR question answering method that decides how to split a view from a measured counting limit of the VLM. Each of its design choices answers a measured limitation. Because the horizon narrows as views grow, the program first fixes the region the question names, which the same pixel budget then shows at a higher resolution. A single view falls short beyond the horizon, so only views counted beyond it are split. Small objects can vanish when a view is downsampled, so a zero from a downsampled view is split as well. A small object is hard to see on the whole image while the place that contains it is not, so the place is grounded first and then the object inside it. The VLM misjudges directions even between marked objects, so a direction is computed from the two boxes with the direction-relation matrix (Goyal and Egenhofer, 2001).

GeoScope differs from earlier work in three ways. First, UHR methods choose where to look from the VLM’s own confidence or attention and take the final answer from the VLM. In GeoScope a spatial program parsed from the question fixes the region, and the VLM provides only local observations. Second, counting by splitting is not new (Xiong et al., 2023; Amini-Naieni and Zisserman, 2026; Qharabagh et al., 2026), but earlier methods either rely on a trained counter or split once. GeoScope splits on a measured property of a frozen VLM, and the response model estimates in advance what a split does. Third, GeoScope keeps the typed spatial programs and executor of our earlier GeoSelect (Jiang et al., 2026b), which addresses referring image segmentation. What it adds is perception only through a frozen VLM and all the perception design above. The programs are written by a frozen, text-only language model that sees neither the image nor the options, so a program depends on the question alone.

We evaluate GeoScope on three UHR benchmarks, making all design choices on development questions and reporting on held-out ones, and reproduce four recent training-free methods with their official code. On the regional counting (RC) and object spatial relationship (OSR) tasks of XLRS-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b), GeoScope improves Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025a) by 16.3 and 10.5 points. On the counting task of MME-RealWorld remote sensing (Zhang et al., 2025b) it gains 11.4 points. Each gain is larger than that of any reproduced method over its own backbone. On UHR-Micro (Ni et al., 2026), which scores a count by its error, it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points and is above MAP, the benchmark’s own training-free method. Its results on XLRS-Bench RC, on the whole of XLRS-Bench by question over all 3,080 questions and, with InternVL3.5-8B, on UHR-Micro regional counting are the highest reported, trained methods included.

Ablations show that the three benchmarks test different limits of the VLM (Section 6.4). On UHR-Micro global counting, where scenes are dense and a count is scored by its error, subdivision adds 15.6 of the 16.8 points. On regional counting in XLRS-Bench and UHR-Micro the gain comes mostly from the window that the program fixes, and on spatial relations from the direction computed from the boxes. MME-RealWorld counting also exposes an option bias. The option stating that the image does not show the number is correct for 5 of the 1,226 questions, yet the backbones choose it for 18 to 57% of the test questions. We therefore also compare with each backbone restricted to the numeric options (Section 7.1). This restricted backbone alone significantly beats every reproduced method run on the whole test split, while GeoScope is level with it with Qwen3-VL-8B and significantly above it with Qwen3-VL-4B.

Our contributions are:

  • 1.

    (C1) The counting horizon and its response model. Measuring frozen VLMs as one calibrates a sensor, we find that eight open VLMs from three families fall increasingly short once a view holds more objects than their counting horizon, which moves with the size of the view, the apparent size of the objects and the imagery. A power-law response model predicts how much of the undercount a split recovers and how many spurious counts it adds. It holds on a second set of crops and across models, and supports the rule of splitting only views counted beyond the horizon.

  • 2.

    (C2) GeoScope. A training-free method for UHR question answering whose design follows from the measured limits of the VLM. A spatial program parsed from the question fixes the region, the VLM grounds and counts only within its operating range, views counted beyond the horizon are split, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. On XLRS-Bench and MME-RealWorld it improves its backbone more than any reproduced training-free method, and on UHR-Micro it is above the benchmark’s own training-free method with the same backbone.

  • 3.

    (C3) Sources of the gains and a benchmark bias. Ablations attribute the gains to the region, subdivision and the computed directions. MME-RealWorld counting scores depend strongly on an option that is almost never correct and on where the correct number sits among the options, and we discuss what a benchmark needs in order to tell counting methods apart (Section 7.1).

2 Related work

2.1 Remote sensing VQA

Trained task-specific networks answer remote sensing questions, including counting questions, on images of about a thousand pixels on a side (Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) and on paired optical and SAR images (Zhao et al., 2025). Remote sensing assistants instruction-tune a VLM on remote sensing data for captioning and VQA, most of them also for grounding (Hu et al., 2025; Kuckreja et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Muhtar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Zhan et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024; Soni et al., 2025). Remote sensing foundation models pre-train image encoders on large image collections, by masked image modelling (Sun et al., 2023) or by aligning images with text, as RemoteCLIP (Liu et al., 2024b) does, and are fine-tuned or probed for each task. RemoteCLIP also introduces a counting benchmark. Further work trains grounding networks and VLMs for grounding and reasoning segmentation, often with reinforcement learning (Choudhury et al., 2025; Shabbir et al., 2025b; An et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d; Jiang et al., 2027). On XLRS-Bench, GeoChat scores below every general VLM evaluated alongside it, and EarthDial below most of them (Wang et al., 2025a; Dang et al., 2026).

XLRS-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b) asks perception and reasoning questions, including regional counting and object spatial relationships, on images of up to 10,000×10,00010{,}000\times 10{,}000 pixels. MME-RealWorld (Zhang et al., 2025b) asks about object position, colour and count in large aerial scenes. RSHR-Bench (Dang et al., 2025) adds further UHR scenes, and UHR-Micro (Ni et al., 2026) asks about objects that cover on average less than 0.01% of the image. Trained approaches extend the input with token pruning (Wang et al., 2025a) or compress tokens under a budget (Dang et al., 2026). Others learn to zoom, crop or call tools through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026c; Zhu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a), adapt to the ground sampling distance of the input with gated low-rank adapters (Zhang et al., 2026a), or self-distil from a teacher with privileged evidence (Jiang et al., 2026a). All of them answer from their own perception of the image or of the views they select.

2.2 Training-free high-resolution perception

ZoomEye searches a zoom tree (Shen et al., 2025), RAP retrieves query-relevant crops and reassembles them (Wang et al., 2025e), DC2 divides and merges patch descriptions (Wang et al., 2025c), and ViCrop crops where attention points (Zhang et al., 2025a). In remote sensing, ImageRAG retrieves patches for an answering model that it fine-tunes lightly (Zhang et al., 2025c), and RADAR localises from attention (Liu et al., 2026d). ZoomSearch searches a tree of 3×\times3 splits scored by a visual retriever and the VLM’s confidence (Zhou et al., 2025). WeaveEarth selects evidence tiles (Ma et al., 2026b). GazeEarth gazes at no more than two cells of a 4×\times4 grid and answers from a foveated warp (Zhang et al., 2026c), and MAP builds and refines a spatially grounded state of local evidence (Ni et al., 2026). These methods decide where the model looks; none uses a measured limit of the VLM to decide when a view must be split.

2.3 Programs, tools and agents

VisProg and ViperGPT compose vision modules into programs written by a language model (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023). DiSciPLE searches with a language model for interpretable programs that predict scientific variables, such as population density, from satellite imagery (Mall et al., 2025). Geode has a language model write code over geospatial data and retrieval services (Gupta et al., 2024), and Change-Agent lets a language model write Python over the outputs of trained change models (Liu et al., 2024a). RS-Agent and ThinkGeo plan and benchmark tool calls (Xu et al., 2026; Shabbir et al., 2025a), IC-EO generates auditable Earth-observation code (Lahouel et al., 2026), and QVLM writes code over the masks of a segmenter trained by its authors (Massih and Cosatto, 2026). GeoPilot and WeaveAgent train models to decide which tools a remote sensing question needs (Zhou et al., 2026a; Pang, 2026), and Bazi et al. (2026) fine-tune a VLM to decide when to call deterministic change-analysis tools. GeoScout-Agent lets a proprietary model zoom, sharpen, run code and segment (Dev et al., 2026). GaiaAgent coordinates language-model agents around a trained change-detection model (Wang et al., 2026d), and BEDI benchmarks VLM-based agents on drones (Guo et al., 2026). Changes between two images can also be captioned without training, by having a text-only language model compare the VLM’s description of each (Ricci et al., 2026). Concurrently with this work, TerraAgent wraps a frozen remote sensing model with agents that split a question and route its parts to perception tools (Huang et al., 2026). Our previous work, GeoSelect (Jiang et al., 2026b), compiles referring expressions into typed spatial programs that are checked and executed deterministically. GeoScope keeps this scaffold, but perceives only through a frozen VLM and derives its counting procedure from a measured property of that VLM.

2.4 Counting limits of VLMs

Humans enumerate small sets at a glance and estimate larger ones (Kaufman et al., 1949). VLMs fail beyond a few objects (Paiss et al., 2023; Campbell et al., 2024; Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024), also on a unified counting benchmark of real images (Rong et al., 2026), and diverge beyond the subitising range on synthetic boards (Pang et al., 2026). They underestimate large numerosities (Testolin et al., 2025; Zhao and Li, 2026) and favour round numbers such as 5 and 10 (Pothiraj et al., 2025). List-then-count and decomposition prompts, pointing and reasoning do not consistently improve counting without training (Alghisi et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2025). Diagnostic benchmarks list counting beyond the subitising range among the cognitive biases of VLMs (Sar et al., 2026), and show that models fall back on object priors against the visual evidence (Alzahrani et al., 2026).

Probing studies locate the failure inside the model. Numerosity is linearly decodable early in the vision encoder, while performance differences follow the language model (Fu et al., 2026). A counting circuit shared across visual reasoning tasks yields precise counts for small numbers and noisy estimates for large ones (Che et al., 2026b). As objects multiply, attention compression erodes the separation between the representations of neighbouring counts, which a fine-tuned convolutional module alleviates (Che et al., 2026a). These works measure or explain the limit. Dedicated open-world counters such as CountGD are trained on counting data and take a text or exemplar prompt (Amini-Naieni et al., 2024). Remote sensing counters regress density maps of dense scenes and are trained to generalise across domains (Liu et al., 2026c). Other methods work around the limit by splitting. SS-DCNet divides dense regions until sub-region counts fall within the closed set its counter has seen (Xiong et al., 2023). CountGD++ crops the image adaptively once it has counted at least 800 objects (Amini-Naieni and Zisserman, 2026), and LVLM-Count cuts an image once into object-aware sub-images (Qharabagh et al., 2026). We instead decide when to split a view from a model of how a split changes a frozen VLM’s answer, tested on aerial imagery.

3 Counting horizon of frozen VLMs

3.1 Measurement on aerial crops

3.1.1 Setup

We cut square crops 256 to 4,096 pixels on a side, clipped where the image is smaller, from a pool of 260 DOTA-v1.5 training images (Xia et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2022). No image that appears in XLRS-Bench or MME-RealWorld is used, and neither these crops nor the FAIR1M and DIOR crops used below come from an image of a UHR-Micro test question. Each crop is centred on cars, trucks, ships or storage tanks, one class per crop, and its ground truth NN is the number of annotated instances of that class in the crop. We draw 60 crops for each of eight bins of NN, from one or two objects to more than 160. Crops are shown at native resolution, with two exceptions: a crop whose long side is below 768 pixels is enlarged to 768, and one with more than 204822048^{2} pixels is reduced to that many. The question is the open-ended one the executor uses, which names the class and asks for a single integer (Supplementary Section S3.2). We report the mean signed relative error (n^−N)/N(\hat{n}-N)/N per bin, where n^\hat{n} is the model’s answer. We also count every crop with count-triggered subdivision, which splits a view into four parts, or two if it is elongated, while its answer exceeds a threshold hh and sums the answers of the parts (Section 4.4). Besides four Qwen-VL models (Bai et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025b) we test InternVL3.5-4B and 8B (Wang et al., 2025d) and LLaVA-OneVision-7B (LLaVA-OV-7B) (Li et al., 2025a). For Qwen3-VL-8B we also draw a second set of crops with another seed, on which the model of Section 3.2 is tested with its exponent fitted on the first. We also show its crops at a budget of 102421024^{2} pixels, which changes only those larger than 1,024 pixels. Qwen3-VL-32B, queried through an API, is shown for reference. In Fig. 3 the band around Qwen3-VL-8B is a bootstrap interval over the 960 crops of both sets, and bins with fewer than eight crops are left out of panel (c).

3.1.2 Findings

Pooled over both sets of crops, the error of Qwen3-VL-8B stays within 15% for up to five objects and turns systematically negative beyond, down to −57-57% above 160 objects (Fig. 3a). Beyond about five objects most answers are undercounts, and many are round numbers. On sets of up to 20 objects, neither listing every instance before counting nor the reasoning variant Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking is significantly more exact, and asking for one box per object degenerates into long lists (Supplementary Section S2.3). The shortfall also depends on the view (Fig. 3c). Crops of 256 pixels, shown enlarged threefold, stay within 21% up to 160 objects, while crops of 2,048 pixels at native resolution fall short at every number of objects. Our denser crops are also larger, so panels (a) and (b) confound the number of objects with the size of the view and of the objects in it.

The other models show the same pattern with different onsets (Table 1). Most fall short by more than 20% from the bin of 6 to 10 objects onward, Qwen3-VL-2B already from three to five, and InternVL3.5, which overcounts small sets, only beyond 40. At the same number of objects, every model falls short more in views of 2,048 pixels than of 256 pixels, InternVL3.5-8B only slightly (Supplementary Section S2.2). We call the number of objects up to which a model counts a view with little bias, before the onset in Table 1, its counting horizon. Pooled over our DOTA crops it is about five.

3.1.3 Other imagery

We repeated the measurement with Qwen3-VL-8B on FAIR1M (Sun et al., 2022) and DIOR (Li et al., 2020), two aerial detection datasets used by neither XLRS-Bench nor MME-RealWorld, and on VisDrone drone images (Zhu et al., 2022), whose objects are larger in pixels (Fig. 4). FAIR1M and DIOR give 480 and 445 crops of at most 1,500 pixels on a side, against up to 4,096 on DOTA. The shortfall appears on all three but sets in later than on DOTA. FAIR1M cars fall short by more than 20% beyond 20 objects, though not monotonically, and DIOR ships only above 160. On VisDrone the error stays within 15% up to 40 objects. Once the VisDrone images are downsampled threefold, the error is negative in every bin and passes −20-20% beyond 20. Subdivision with the horizon measured on DOTA removes most of the shortfall on FAIR1M cars and full-detail VisDrone, and part of it at reduced detail. On DIOR ships it adds a surplus of up to 15%, the spurious counts of views split while still within the horizon (Section 3.2). For FAIR1M trucks and DIOR vehicles the annotation does not match the question we ask (Supplementary Section S2.5). The horizon thus depends on the imagery, including the size of its views, as well as on the model. GeoScope uses the horizon measured on DOTA, the source of 96% of the MME-RealWorld counting images (Supplementary Section S6.4).

3.2 Response model of splitting

The measurements suggest a simple model of a single view. Let a view contain nn objects of the queried class and let c⁡(n)c(n) be the expected answer. We model

c⁡(n)=a​nγ(n≥1),c⁡(0)=s,c(n)=a\,n^{\gamma}\ \ (n\geq 1),\qquad c(0)=s, (1)

with 0<γ≤10<\gamma\leq 1 and a spurious answer s≥0s\geq 0 for an empty view. Near the horizon c⁡(n)≈nc(n)\approx n, matching the unbiased small counts, while for large nn the answer is only a fraction a​nγ−1a\,n^{\gamma-1} of the true count. Fitted by least squares on logarithms, which recovers γ\gamma under multiplicative noise, on unsplit crops with more than five objects and a non-zero answer, the exponent is 0.76 for Qwen3-VL-8B on its first set and lies between 0.43 and 0.80 for the other models (Table 1). Pooled over crop sizes, the exponent also absorbs the loss of small objects in large views; fitted within each crop size up to 2,048 pixels, that of Qwen3-VL-8B is closer to one (Supplementary Section S1). Eq. (1) is a descriptive model of the answers on such crops, which we use to predict what a split does to them.

Proposition 1 (Split amplification).

Split a view holding n≥1n\geq 1 objects into parts holding n1,…,nKn_{1},\dots,n_{K} objects, ∑knk=n\sum_{k}n_{k}=n, of which mm are empty. Under Eq. (1), with the same aa, γ\gamma and ss for the parts as for the view, the expected sum of the parts’ answers is

∑k=1Kc(nk)=c(n)∑k:nk>0(nkn)γ+ms,\sum_{k=1}^{K}c(n_{k})\;=\;c(n)\,\sum_{k:\,n_{k}>0}\Big(\frac{n_{k}}{n}\Big)^{\gamma}\;+\;m\,s, (2)

and the amplification A=∑k(nk/n)γA=\sum_{k}(n_{k}/n)^{\gamma} satisfies 1≤A≤K1−γ1\leq A\leq K^{1-\gamma}. For γ<1\gamma<1, A=1A=1 only when all objects fall into one part.

Proof.

Eq. (2) follows from Eq. (1) term by term. The bounds hold because x↦xγx\mapsto x^{\gamma} is concave and zero at zero, hence subadditive, and its sum over KK shares is largest when the shares are equal (A). ∎

A split therefore raises an undercounted answer by a factor fixed by how the objects divide, unless all objects fall into one part, and adds ss for every empty part. Recursion shrinks the undercount of every part, but the spurious term grows with the number of empty parts. A view already within the horizon gains nothing from a split, so splitting should be triggered by the answer.

3.2.1 Validation of the model

Every part of the crops has a recorded answer, so the model can be checked at each split of the recursion of Section 4.4. We compare the ratio of the parts’ summed answers to the parent’s answer with the amplification AA, computed from the true counts of the parts and the exponent of the same model in Table 1 (Fig. 5). For Qwen3-VL-8B the two agree within 0.08 in every bin of parents from 6 to 160 objects. On its second set of crops, with the exponent of the first set, they agree within 0.10 in four of five bins. For the seven other models the observed amplification lies mostly within 20% of the prediction (Supplementary Section S1). Empty parts are answered with 0.8 to 2.4 spurious objects on average (column ss of Table 1). Above 160 objects the observed amplification is about 2.1, far above the predicted 1.3. Here the parts also reveal objects too small to see in the parent, a limit of resolution that is separate from the undercount.

3.2.2 Comparison with fixed grids

Fixed grids, tiles of bounded size and subdivision with hh from 20 down to 1 are compared on the same answers of Qwen3-VL-8B, given for every part of the 937 crops of both sets down to the 256-pixel cell (Fig. 6; Supplementary Section S1). Over all crops a 4×\times4 grid and subdivision at h=5h=5 cost about the same, 9.0 and 9.4 calls per crop, and neither is significantly more accurate. They differ in where the errors and calls fall. On views with more than 20 objects both about halve the median error of a single view, the grid slightly more and with fewer calls. On views with fewer objects, fixed grids overcount, the more so the finer they are. For one or two objects a 4×\times4 grid answers 2.6 times the truth on average, while subdivision stays within 10% of the truth at every number of objects up to 160 (Fig. 6b). Up to 20 objects it spends 2.7 calls per crop, against 7.3 for the grid. Tiles of at most 512 pixels are as accurate with 8.1 calls, but their number grows with the area, to about 400 for a whole image of 10,000 pixels on a side. Table 2 repeats the comparison on the second set, with zeros from downsampled views also split, and Section 6.4 inside GeoScope.

3.2.3 Comparison with open-vocabulary detectors

Counting the boxes of three open-vocabulary detectors does worse than either the grid or subdivision (Table 2). They count the same crops with the same class phrase, in tiles enlarged twofold, at a threshold chosen on the first DOTA set (Zhao et al., 2024; Minderer et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2025). They overcount views with few objects. In views with more than 160 objects, two of them miss about half or more of the objects on every set, and OWLv2 does so on DIOR ships. Only OWLv2 on DIOR ships, in small images, is level with subdivision in median error, and its total error there is more than twice as large (Supplementary Section S2.6).

Splitting helps even when its leaves still hold more than hh objects. Nine in ten objects in our crops end in such leaves, yet each split recovers the share of the undercount that Proposition 1 predicts. A fixed grid recovers as much on dense views but overcounts sparse ones, which most counting questions concern (Section 7.1). GeoScope therefore splits only views whose answer exceeds the horizon or that answer zero at reduced resolution, and stops at a minimum cell (Section 4.4).

4 GeoScope

4.1 Overview

Given a UHR image II, a question qq and answer options 𝒪\mathcal{O}, GeoScope answers as

π\displaystyle\pi =Synthesise​(q),\displaystyle=\textsc{Synthesise}(q),
r\displaystyle r =Execute​(π,I,V),\displaystyle=\textsc{Execute}(\pi,I;\,V),
o^\displaystyle\hat{o} =Match​(r,𝒪).\displaystyle=\textsc{Match}(r,\mathcal{O}).

A frozen, text-only language model writes a typed program π\pi from the question alone. A deterministic executor runs it on the image, and the executed result rr is matched to the values of the options, not to their letters, to give the answer o^\hat{o}. Neither the synthesiser nor the VLM VV sees the options, and no parameter is updated. GeoScope takes from GeoSelect (Jiang et al., 2026b) the typed programs, their type checking and the stepwise fallbacks. What GeoScope adds is how the executor uses the VLM, set by the measurements of Section 3. It asks the VLM only for local judgements: grounding a phrase in a view where the target is visible, and counting a class in a view that is split while its count exceeds the horizon. It chooses each view and its resolution, grounds a place before the objects inside it, and computes every direction and distance from the grounded boxes. Fig. 2a shows the three stages, and Fig. 2b and c two test questions. For the counting question the program fixes the lower-right part of the image, and the executor splits it while the VLM’s count exceeds five. For the relation question it grounds the residential area, then both objects inside the area’s window, and computes the direction from their boxes. The backbone’s own answer is wrong in both cases.

4.2 Typed programs

A program is an expression tree over four types: sets of boxes, image regions, counts and directions. Its abstract syntax is

prog ::= count(set) | direction(set, set)
set ::= detect(class) | ref | in_region(set, region)
| filter(set, dir, set) | near(set, set) | top1(set)
| argmax(set, key) | argmin(set, key)
ref ::= refer(expr [, class] [, plural] [, within=(ref | part(dir))])
region ::= image | red_circle | part(dir) | around(set)
dir ::= TOP | BOTTOM | LEFT | RIGHT | UL | UR | LL | LR | CENTER
key ::= X | Y | AREA | LENGTH

A counting question becomes a count over a set. The set is described by a short class phrase that keeps the question’s colour and shape words, such as red car, and is restricted to a region of the image or to the surroundings of an anchor object. A relation question becomes a direction between two referents. Each referent keeps the object’s own referring expression, its class, whether it denotes several objects and, when the question names one, the place or image part that contains it. The synthesiser writes the program from this grammar and a few worked examples, and a checker rejects programs that are not well typed. The full grammar, in the JSON form that the synthesiser writes, and the evaluation of each operator are given in Supplementary Section S3.1. For MME-RealWorld counting, a program that the checker rejects or that drops a colour, shape, place or position word of the question is written once more (Supplementary Section S3.2).

4.3 Perception by a frozen VLM

The VLM is called only to ground a phrase in a window, returning boxes, or to count a class in a window, returning an integer. Every call renders its window at a fixed pixel budget BB, so a large window is downsampled; we call the rendered window a view. Grounding in a large window is therefore coarse to fine, and candidate boxes found in the downsampled window are confirmed in close-ups at near-native resolution. A referring expression is grounded as a whole, so that the VLM resolves its attributes and local relations, and the box is then refined with the class phrase.

Small objects are often named through the place that contains them, as in “the grey tennis court in the residential area right of centre”. The place is visible on the whole image when the object is not, so GeoScope resolves such a referent hierarchically. It grounds the place on the whole image and then the object inside a window around the place, which the same budget renders at a much higher resolution.

4.4 Count-triggered subdivision

A counting program fixes a region, and the VLM counts the class inside it. Enumerating boxes degenerates in dense views, so GeoScope counts grounded boxes only for sets that the executor cannot turn into a class phrase and one window, mostly a filter or near nested inside a region. This happens in 51 of the 962 MME-RealWorld counting programs executed on the test split (Supplementary Section S3.3). Algorithm 1 applies the rules of Section 3.2. A view’s count is accepted if it lies within the horizon hh. The one exception is a zero from a downsampled view, since objects too small to see at a coarse scale may still be present. Any other view is split into four parts, or two if it is elongated. Each part is counted in the same way down to a minimum cell, and the counts of the leaves, the parts not split further, are summed. In Algorithm 1, |w||w| is the area of window ww in pixels, so the view is downsampled when ζ>1\zeta>1; side⁡(w)\mathrm{side}(w) is its longer side, dd its depth in the recursion, and Split returns the four or two parts.

We use one threshold, h=5h=5, with every backbone. It is the upper end of the last bin before the shortfall of most models in Table 1, read off the measurement rather than tuned. For Qwen3-VL-8B the exact value matters little. On the DOTA crops of Section 3, h=3h=3, 5 and 8 give median absolute relative errors of 0.37, 0.35 and 0.33 (Supplementary Section S1), and on development counting questions of MME-RealWorld, in an earlier configuration that still accepted zeros from downsampled views, 40.4, 41.2 and 41.2% accuracy (Supplementary Section S6.8). For InternVL3.5-8B, whose shortfall on DOTA begins beyond 40 objects, h=40h=40 is not better on UHR-Micro (Section 7.3). Once zeros from downsampled views are split, few views with more than ten objects are left unsplit (Supplementary Section S1). The regions of XLRS-Bench RC are small drawn circles, so their crop is counted in a single view.

4.5 Geometry, option matching and fallbacks

The direction of one box relative to another is computed from the direction-relation matrix (Goyal and Egenhofer, 2001). It tiles the plane around the reference box and weights each tile’s direction by how much of the target falls in it. Unlike the angle between box centres, it respects the extent of objects, so an object directly above a wide building is above it even if its centre lies left of the building’s centre. A count selects the option value with the highest Poisson likelihood when the count is taken as the mean, and a direction selects the option closest in angle. On RC, a count that equals no option value is taken twice more, from a wider and from an enlarged view, and Match uses the median of the three. The VLM still never sees the options, and RC accuracy is the same without this step (Supplementary Section S3.3). Execution degrades in steps instead of failing. If an anchor or place of a counting program is not found, it is searched for again without its colour and shape words and then also without its own constraints. A referent of a relation question that yields no box is grounded by its class phrase. As a last resort the question receives the VLM’s own answer (Supplementary Section S3.3). With Qwen3-VL-8B, more than 95% of the RC, OSR and MME-RealWorld counting questions are answered by an executed program.

Some questions are answered without a synthesised program. A question that gives a pixel box is answered by a fixed program. XLRS-Bench gives one for the category, colour and motion state of an object, and the VLM answers from the whole image together with a close-up in which the box is outlined. UHR-Micro gives one for the region of a regional counting question, which is then counted as in Section 4.4. It marks the two objects of its direction and distance questions with coloured rectangles, from whose boxes the relation is computed (Section 6.3). Position and colour questions of MME-RealWorld are answered by the VLM directly.

5 Experimental setup

5.1 Benchmarks and protocol

We evaluate on three benchmarks (Table 3). From the lite release of XLRS-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b) we use regional counting (RC), about regions drawn as red circles, and object spatial relationship (OSR); the other subtasks, among them overall counting of ships or cars in a whole scene, enter its overall score. From MME-RealWorld-RS (MME-RS), the remote sensing part of MME-RealWorld (Zhang et al., 2025b), GeoScope answers the counting questions and its backbone the position and colour questions. UHR-Micro (Ni et al., 2026) has its own splits (Section 6.3).

All design choices are made on a seeded 20% development split of each task; the configuration is frozen before any test evaluation, and the remaining 80% form the held-out test split. Gains are paired on the same questions, with 95% bootstrap intervals over questions (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993).

5.2 Baselines

The zero-shot baseline is the frozen VLM answering the multiple-choice question from the whole image at 4 M pixels, taking the option letter with the highest first-token score. With this protocol Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 74.46, 63.98 and 25.45 on all MME-RealWorld position, colour and counting questions, against 56.41, 48.07 and 21.35 reported elsewhere (Ma et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c; Jiang et al., 2026a). Our zero-shot reference is stronger mainly because the image is given at a larger size (Supplementary Section S4.3), and GazeEarth’s own direct baseline, run on our test questions, comes within 3.0 points of it on position (Supplementary Section S5.4). MME-RealWorld counting questions also offer the option stating that the image does not show the number. It is correct for 5 of the 1,226 questions, yet the four backbones we ran zero-shot choose it for 18 to 57% of the test questions. We therefore also report each backbone restricted to the numeric options, answering with the numeric option of highest first-token score. This raises Qwen3-VL-8B from 25.45 to 35.64 on all counting questions.

The constant-answer baseline always picks the option position or option-value rank, such as option B or the largest number, that is most often correct on the development split, with ties broken in its favour on the test split (Supplementary Section S4.4).

5.3 Reproduced methods

For every task we reproduce, with its official code, the training-free method whose reported result is the strongest: WeaveEarth (Ma et al., 2026b) for RC, GazeEarth (Zhang et al., 2026c) for OSR and XLRS-Bench as a whole, and ZoomSearch (Zhou et al., 2025) and RAP (Wang et al., 2025e) for MME-RealWorld counting. Each method runs its own pipeline, including its own answer extraction, on our test questions, and its gain is measured against the zero-shot answers of its own backbone. The backbone is Qwen3-VL-8B for WeaveEarth, GazeEarth and RAP, and LLaVA-OV-7B for ZoomSearch and for a second run of RAP on a fixed 20% subset of the counting questions. Their settings are given in Supplementary Section S5. Where other papers have re-run these methods on our tasks, their numbers are mostly close to ours or lower, and lower than the numbers the methods report for themselves (Supplementary Section S5.3). We also re-run one trained method, Text-Before-Vision (Wang et al., 2026a), with its released checkpoint and code on all XLRS-Bench questions (Supplementary Section S5.5). It is the only published method that reports a higher XLRS-Bench average than GeoScope.

5.4 Implementation details

GeoScope uses Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) as the synthesiser and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a) as the perception model, both decoding greedily. The pixel budget BB is 2.5 M pixels, 1 M pixels for RC crops and 4 M pixels for XLRS-Bench overall counting. Counting uses h=5h=5, a depth limit D=5D=5 and a minimum cell of μ=256\mu=256 pixels. A counted window is enlarged by 15% on each side, since grounded places are coarse and objects on their border would otherwise be cut; this does not bias the counts upward (Section 7.1). A window longer than 7,000 pixels is first cut into equal cells; the images of XLRS-Bench overall counting are cut into cells of 2,000 pixels. Every experiment runs on one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 with 24 GiB of memory, except the re-run of Text-Before-Vision, which its script serves on two GPUs, and Qwen3-VL-32B, which we query through an API.

6 Results

6.1 Comparison with reproduced training-free methods

Against its own backbone on the same test questions (Table 4), GeoScope improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on RC, 10.5 on OSR and 11.4 on MME-RealWorld counting, all significantly. No reproduced method gains as much on any task. WeaveEarth and GazeEarth stay close to their backbone on RC and OSR, and WeaveEarth gains 5.3 points on counting. ZoomSearch improves OSR but not counting, and RAP gains 5.2 points on counting. RAP with LLaVA-OV-7B was run only on a fixed 20% subset of the counting questions, where GeoScope scores 29.95 with Qwen3-VL-8B and 30.96 with LLaVA-OV-7B, against 35.53 for RAP. MME-RealWorld counting also rewards a fixed guess. Always choosing option B beats zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B, no reproduced method run on the whole split exceeds it, and GeoScope exceeds it by 5.1 points (Section 7.1).

GeoScope also gains on the other three backbones, though not significantly on OSR with Qwen2.5-VL-7B or on counting with LLaVA-OV-7B. The gains grow with the weaker Qwen3-VL-4B, which matches the 8B system on counting and comes within four points of it on RC and OSR. On LLaVA-OV-7B, the backbone of ZoomSearch and RAP, GeoScope is significantly above ZoomSearch on RC, by 21.3 points, and level with it on OSR and counting.

Table 5 splits the counting questions by where the correct number sits among the options, leaving out the RAP run on part of the split. For 222 questions the answer is the largest number offered. A count that falls short picks a smaller number there. GeoScope with Qwen3-VL-8B answers 58.1% of these questions correctly, against 5.4% for its zero-shot backbone and at most 23.4% for a reproduced method. The other 759 questions mostly ask about at most five objects. On them the reproduced methods and GeoScope all score between 29 and 39, and Qwen3-VL-8B restricted to the numeric options does best. Against its backbone restricted in this way, GeoScope therefore gains only on the questions whose answer is the largest number offered, with every backbone; part of that gain is owed to the layout (Section 7.1).

6.2 Comparison with published results

Published numbers cover all questions of each task, so Table 6 gives GeoScope on all questions as well as on the held-out 80%. GeoChat (Kuckreja et al., 2024), EarthDial (Soni et al., 2025), GeoLLaVA-8K (Wang et al., 2025a), UHR-BAT (Dang et al., 2026) and ScaleEarth (Zhang et al., 2026a) are fine-tuned. GeoEyes (Wang et al., 2026b), GeoLens (Wang et al., 2026c), GeoVista (Zhu et al., 2026), ZoomEarth (Liu et al., 2026a) and Text-Before-Vision (Wang et al., 2026a) add reinforcement learning, and MLRS (Ailuro et al., 2026) uses reinforcement learning alone. RS-OPSD (Jiang et al., 2026a) is self-distilled. DualComp (Li et al., 2026b) trains a router that sets how GeoLLaVA-8K’s tokens are compressed, so we list it as trained. The training-free methods are ZoomEye (Shen et al., 2025), RAP (Wang et al., 2025e), ZoomSearch, WeaveEarth and GazeEarth. Where a paper averages otherwise, we average its reported subtasks. GeoScope answers the position and colour questions of MME-RealWorld with its backbone’s zero-shot answers.

GeoScope has the highest reported accuracy on RC among trained and training-free methods, 63.00 against 55.0 for RS-OPSD. On OSR it reaches 46.40 on all questions and 44.00 on the held-out ones, against 44.8 for UHR-BAT, the best trained model, and 37.80 for GazeEarth, the best training-free method. GeoEyes, GeoLens and GeoVista fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Without training, GeoScope with this backbone is above GeoEyes and GeoLens on both tasks and below GeoVista on OSR.

On XLRS-Bench as a whole, programs answer RC, OSR and overall counting. Questions that give a pixel box are answered as in Section 4.5, and the backbone answers the other seven subtasks. GeoScope then reaches 59.98 averaged over the 13 subtasks, above every published training-free result, and 71.82 over all 3,080 questions, the highest reported by question for any method, trained or not. The close-ups of given pixel boxes add 7.1 of its 11.2 points over the backbone on the average over subtasks and 22.8 of the 26.2 points by question, and the programs for RC, OSR and overall counting add the rest (Supplementary Section S6.1). GazeEarth reports 53.51 by question. Run with its official code on our held-out questions, it answers 39.61% of them correctly, against 46.71% for zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B and 71.51% for GeoScope. It loses most on questions about the object in a given box (Supplementary Section S5.3). GeoScope’s average is also above that of every trained method that reports its subtasks. ScaleEarth reports 59.4 (Zhang et al., 2026a), and GeoLens and GeoEyes report 54.2 (Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b).

Only the trained Text-Before-Vision (Wang et al., 2026a) reports a higher average, 60.40, the mean of 32 sampled answers per question, without results per subtask. Table 6 therefore also lists our re-run of its released checkpoint and code, scored like every other method with one answer per question, with greedy and with sampled answers (Supplementary Section S5.5). On the held-out questions the two re-runs reach 50.54 and 48.15, and GeoScope, at 59.53, is 9.0 and 11.4 points above them. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the model Text-Before-Vision is trained from, GeoScope reaches 56.93 on these questions, 6.4 and 8.8 points above, and all four differences are significant.

On MME-RealWorld, GeoScope’s average is the highest among published training-free methods, mostly through the backbone’s position accuracy, and below the trained RS-OPSD. On counting, its 37.93 on all questions is above the 37.4 of RS-OPSD. It is below the 39.15 and 40.25 that ZoomSearch reports for itself and for RAP, both with LLaVA-OV-7B. With that backbone GeoScope reaches 34.67 on all questions and 34.56 on our test split, where ZoomSearch, re-run with its official code, reaches 31.50. Two later papers obtain 20.1 and 17.9 (Ma et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c), and on RC and OSR our reproduction agrees with the values measured by RS-OPSD (Jiang et al., 2026a) (Supplementary Section S5.3). With LLaVA-OV-7B, GeoScope is above ZoomSearch on RC and on the average over subtasks, and level on OSR. Its MME-RealWorld average with that backbone is lower than those of ZoomSearch and RAP, because its position and colour answers are the backbone’s own.

6.3 Results on UHR-Micro

UHR-Micro (Ni et al., 2026) uses images of about 4,800×3,2004{,}800\times 3{,}200 pixels from DOTA, FAIR1M, SODA-A and xView. A count c^\hat{c} of cc objects scores max⁡(0,1−|c^−c|/c)\max(0,1-|\hat{c}-c|/c), so a close count earns partial credit. We evaluate the five task types that GeoScope covers, 1,369 test questions (Table 7). Regional counting questions give the region either as a pixel box, which becomes the program’s region, or in words, as conditional counting questions do. Direction and distance questions mark the two objects with rectangles of fixed colours. The executor finds them by colour, as it finds the red circle of XLRS-Bench RC, and computes the relation from their boxes. We use the configuration of MME-RealWorld counting unchanged and add only the pixel-box region to the program language; the validation split confirmed the 15% margin used on the other benchmarks (Supplementary Section S6.9).

GeoScope improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.8 points on global and 36.2 on regional counting, and is above MAP, the benchmark’s own training-free method, on both. Most of the global gain comes from subdivision. Counting each region in a single unsplit view scores 24.87, close to zero-shot answering, and subdivision adds 15.6 points. On regional counting the unsplit view of the given box already scores 42.43, and subdivision adds 6.9; both gains are significant (Supplementary Section S6.9). InternVL3.5-8B counts better zero-shot, and MAP is also reported with it. With this backbone GeoScope gains 8.2 and 37.7 points, has the highest reported score on regional counting, 58.77 against 57.81 for MAP, and is one point below MAP on global counting.

Conditional counting does not improve significantly with either backbone. Half of these questions ask for a fine-grained aircraft type such as A220, on which GeoScope with Qwen3-VL-8B scores 8.3 and zero-shot answering 3.3. In the others the place is described in words, and when the program grounds the wrong place, the count belongs to another region. Every direction and distance question is answered correctly, because once the marked boxes are found the relation is computed from them.

6.4 Ablation study

A program fixes where to look, grounds objects, splits views and computes geometry, and the benchmarks reward these steps differently. To separate the window from what follows it, we asked the backbone the original question on the window each test program chose (Supplementary Section S6.6). On XLRS-Bench RC it answers as well as the count does, so there the gain comes from the window. The circled regions are small, and a crop shows one at a far higher resolution than the whole image does, the kind of view in which the horizon lies further out (Fig. 3c). Such a crop is counted in a single view. On OSR the computed direction is significantly more accurate, by 6.8 points, than the backbone’s answer on the union of the two referents. Grounding a place before the objects inside it adds 7 development points, and the direction-relation matrix 10 development and 2.0 test points over the centre angle (Table 8). On MME-RealWorld counting the count beats the direct answer on the window by 12.5 points, a significant difference, and the direct answer restricted to the numeric options by 3.2 points, which is not significant. Most of the gain there comes from the window and from answering with a number. Subdivision supplies most of the gain where scenes are dense and a count is scored by its error, as on UHR-Micro global counting (Section 6.3).

Without a program, the whole image is counted with the same procedure, and test accuracy on counting falls from 36.60 to 32.62. GeoScope’s gain over zero-shot answering is 13.5 points on the 859 questions whose program restricts the region, and slightly negative on the 103 about the whole image, whose answers are small.

Both effects that Proposition 1 predicts, the recovered undercount beyond the horizon and the spurious counts below it, appear on MME-RealWorld in the last two columns of Table 8. When the whole image is counted, as in the rows without a program, removing subdivision costs a significant 4.6 points on questions with 6 to 20 objects and gains 2.1 on those with at most five. Accepting zeros from downsampled views has a similar effect. Within the regions that programs name, which already divide the scene, the loss on 6 to 20 objects shrinks to 2.7 points, which is not significant. Most counting questions ask for at most five objects, so the two effects nearly cancel on the whole task. With Qwen3-VL-4B, which undercounts more strongly, removing subdivision costs a significant 2.2 points overall. Since the answer to a dense question is often the largest number offered, these differences also reward erring upwards; UHR-Micro, which scores a count by its relative error, tests the proposition without this bias.

A fixed 4×\times4 grid in place of count-triggered subdivision costs about as many VLM calls and lowers test accuracy by 2.9 points, not significantly. On questions about at most five objects its median count is 2.7 times the truth, while that of subdivision is exact, so it picks the largest number offered about twice as often. It therefore gains significantly on the questions whose answer is the largest number offered and loses on the others. On XLRS-Bench overall counting it needs three times as many calls and answers 10.4 points fewer test questions correctly, again not significantly (Supplementary Section S6.5). Programs written by the VLM, with or without the image, lose four to seven development points (Supplementary Section S3.5).

6.5 Computational cost

GeoScope and zero-shot answering are timed on development questions. GeoScope starts from scratch on each question, and its times include program synthesis. The reproduced methods are timed on the test questions of each task (Fig. 7), and RAP with LLaVA-OV-7B on the fixed subset (Supplementary Section S7). ZoomSearch and RAP swap their two models to fit in 24 GiB, and their times include the swap. GeoScope’s cost depends on how many VLM calls its program makes. An RC question needs about two VLM calls on small crops and costs about as much as zero-shot answering. OSR and counting questions need five and seven calls at the median, with a long tail for dense regions. Synthesis takes one to four seconds per question, and executing a program less than ten milliseconds; almost all the rest goes to VLM calls. On the same GPU, ZoomSearch is 2.8 to 32 times slower than GeoScope and RAP 18 to 37 times. WeaveEarth and GazeEarth are faster on OSR and counting.

Peak GPU memory differs little between methods, because the weights of an 8B backbone take about 16 GiB of it (Fig. 8). GeoScope peaks at 19.3 GiB while it executes programs, about as much as zero-shot answering, and its synthesiser runs as a separate stage at 14.5 GiB. With Qwen3-VL-4B, which matches the 8B system on counting (Section 6.1), program execution needs 9.0 GiB, and the synthesiser stage sets the peak. ZoomSearch and RAP fit on the card only by keeping one of their two models in host memory while the other runs; together with the retriever’s 6.4 GiB they would exceed 24 GiB.

6.6 Qualitative comparison

Figs. 9, 10 and 11 show test questions with the regions each method inspected, from the runs in Tables 4 and 7. The examples are drawn at random: on each benchmark, two questions that GeoScope answers correctly and zero-shot answering does not, and one that it answers wrongly. On UHR-Micro a score of at least 0.8 counts as correct, and the wrong example scores at most 0.3. The search methods pick regions by the VLM’s confidence, and in these examples their regions often miss the small one the question names. GeoScope’s views follow from the program instead: the crop of the red circle, the two referents, or the cells of a split region. Counts are matched to the options as in Section 4.5, so in Fig. 10(a) a count of 2 selects the option 3. One correct answer, in Fig. 10(b), is right for the wrong reason. GeoScope finds no parking lot next to the basketball court, drops the anchor, and counts the red cars of a parking lot at the other end of the image. Among the wrong answers, in Fig. 9(c) the VLM counts four of the five houses and option matching picks 3. In Fig. 10(c) the water is counted in two halves at reduced resolution. Each half reports one buoy, a count within the horizon, so neither is split; the sum of 2 falls one short of 3, and option matching picks 1. In Fig. 11(c) the program places the region beside the hangars, above the parked airplanes it should count.

6.7 Failure analysis

XLRS-Bench overall counting asks how many ships or cars a whole scene holds, typically several dozen. GeoScope lifts zero-shot answering from 10.42 to 35.42, but like every method we ran it does not beat always picking the second-largest of the four numbers, which scores 37.50. Adjacent options lie about 17% apart, so a correct choice needs a count within about 8%, and GeoScope’s counts there are unbiased but scatter by 18% around the truth. Subdivision removes the undercount of Section 3, but not the spurious counts and unresolved objects of many small leaves.

Across tasks, the main remaining error is grounding the wrong object. On OSR, 86% of the wrong answers point more than 45 degrees away from the correct option, which correctly grounded referents would not produce, and counting errors are as often too high as too low (Supplementary Section S8). In a manual check of 150 programs, those that simplify their question are answered correctly about as often as the rest, and hand-written programs change accuracy by at most two of thirty questions per task (Supplementary Section S3.4). Perception limits accuracy more than program synthesis does.

7 Discussion

7.1 Option bias in counting benchmarks

Of the 981 MME-RealWorld counting test questions, 700 concern at most five objects, within the horizon, and only 81 more than ten. Counting dense regions well therefore moves the overall score little, and a procedure that adds spurious counts to sparse regions, as a fixed grid does (Sections 3.2 and 6.4), can lose more than it gains.

The reproduced methods also choose the option stating that the image does not show the number (Section 5.2), for 9 to 18% of the test questions (Table 5; other models in Supplementary Section S6.3). The restricted score of Qwen3-VL-8B, 35.64 on all questions, is above what WeaveEarth and GazeEarth report with this model, and close to the trained RS-OPSD (Table 6). The same restriction brings LLaVA-OV-7B within two points of what ZoomSearch reports for itself and for RAP with this model, while ZoomSearch’s table lists the model itself at 27.57. On our test split, every reproduced method run on the whole split falls significantly below the restricted answers of its own backbone. ZoomSearch, which runs on LLaVA-OV-7B, is also significantly below those of Qwen3-VL-8B, by 4.0 points. GeoScope is level with them with three backbones and above them with Qwen3-VL-4B. Counting gains on this benchmark therefore depend strongly on how often the backbone picks the option stating that the image does not show the number. Comparing with the backbone restricted to the numeric options controls for this.

Where the correct number sits among the options also matters. It is the largest number offered for 52% of the test questions about 6 to 10 objects and 41% of those about 11 to 20, but never for one or two objects. A method that undercounts dense scenes can rarely answer these questions, and one that overcounts gains on them whether or not its count is close. The 15% margin around a counted window does not make GeoScope overcount. In windows with the margin its counts are too high for 274 test questions and too low for 226, about as in whole-image windows without it, 120 and 91. Without the margin, development accuracy falls from 43.3 to 37.6; as many counts are too high as before, and more are too low (Supplementary Section S6.8). On UHR-Micro, whose score penalises overcounts, the margin raised the development score from 45.34 to 48.30 (Supplementary Section S6.9).

XLRS-Bench overall counting has a different problem. Its scenes hold dozens of objects, but its options lie closer together than any method we ran can count (Section 6.7). To tell counting procedures apart, a benchmark would need questions spread over the whole range of counts, and options spaced in proportion to the count and placed at random around it. It would also need to drop any option that is almost never correct.

7.2 Scope of the program language

For the position and colour questions of MME-RealWorld we built programs that locate the object and read its position from geometry or name its colour on a close-up. They were to replace the backbone only if they beat it by at least five points on the development split, a rule set before they were run. They reached 74.9 against 73.7 for the backbone on position, not a significant difference, and 60.6 against 65.7 on colour, so these questions go to the backbone. The program language has types for sets of boxes, image regions, counts and directions, but none for land cover, time or paths. Land use, anomaly and environmental reasoning, route planning and change questions therefore lie outside it. Even within its scope, 43 of the 245 development counting questions use constructions the grammar lacks, such as ordinals, between or the state of an object. They are answered by simplified programs, with 51.2% accuracy against 41.6% for the rest (Supplementary Section S3.4). Questions about change or about measurement in physical units would need types for time and for units.

7.3 Ground sampling distance and other imagery

Whether a VLM can count a view depends on how many pixels each object covers as shown, and also on the extent of the view (Section 3.1). The pixel size of an object follows from the ground sampling distance (GSD) and the scale at which the view is rendered. A car 4.5 m long spans 15 pixels at a GSD of 0.3 m. Rendered whole at 2.5 M pixels, a scene of 10,000 pixels on a side is reduced 6.3-fold, and the car spans about two pixels. A 256-pixel cell of the same scene, enlarged to 768 pixels, shows it at about 45. Larger apparent objects account for part of the later onset of the horizon on FAIR1M, DIOR and VisDrone (Fig. 4); on VisDrone, object size alone does not explain it (Supplementary Section S2.4). Measuring the horizon takes a few hundred crops with annotated counts, binned by the number of objects; we used 373 to 480 per dataset. In our experiments GeoScope uses h=5h=5 for every backbone and dataset. A threshold for a given model and imagery could instead be estimated once in this way, on the imagery it is used for. For InternVL3.5-8B, the threshold of 40 measured on DOTA raises UHR-Micro global counting by 1.8 points and lowers regional counting by 1.9, because its single views of UHR-Micro already fall short below 40 objects (Supplementary Section S6.9). GeoScope’s programs, prompts and executor do not depend on the imagery.

7.4 Generality beyond remote sensing

Every model we tested falls short beyond some number of objects, with an onset that depends on the model and, for Qwen3-VL-8B, on the imagery (Section 3.1), and recent probing studies locate the limit inside the VLM (Fu et al., 2026; Che et al., 2026a). Our measurements, however, are confined to aerial and drone images of a few object classes, and Proposition 1 is tested only there. Whether the same response curve and the same predictable gain from splitting hold for crowds, cells or everyday scenes, and whether the horizon follows the architecture or the distribution of numbers in the training data, remain open. GeoScope’s counting procedure takes the horizon as a single threshold, so it can be applied in such a study by setting hh from a measurement on the new imagery.

8 Conclusion

Frozen VLMs fall increasingly short when an aerial view holds more than a few objects of a class, about five on DOTA for most of the models we tested. Where this horizon lies depends on the view, the objects and the imagery. A simple model of the answers predicts what a split recovers and what it adds, and motivates splitting only views counted beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a deterministic executor runs typed programs, chooses the views and asks the VLM only to ground and count in them. It improves Qwen3-VL-8B on XLRS-Bench regional counting, spatial relations and MME-RealWorld counting more than any reproduced training-free method improves its own backbone, and it has the highest reported accuracy, trained or not, on XLRS-Bench regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro, which scores counts by their error, subdivision alone adds 15.6 points to global counting, while on regional counting most of the gain comes from the window that the program fixes. On MME-RealWorld counting, an option that is almost never correct distorts comparisons. Barred from it, the backbone alone significantly beats every reproduced method run on all test questions, and GeoScope is level with it or above it.

GeoScope leaves to its backbone the position and colour questions without a pixel box, and questions on land use and reasoning. Whole-scene counts with closely spaced options need a more precise counting primitive than a single VLM view (Section 6.7). A wrongly grounded place gives a count for the wrong region, which limits GeoScope on the conditional counting of UHR-Micro (Section 6.3).

More broadly, measuring where a frozen model can be trusted and computing everything else explicitly from what it grounds improves answers without task-specific training.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 1

The proof uses Eq. (1) through one assumption only. The expected answer to a view depends only on the number of objects of the queried class in it. A part holding nkn_{k} objects is therefore expected to be answered with c⁡(nk)c(n_{k}), whatever its size and position. This holds only approximately, since a smaller part shows its objects larger (Section 3.1). Eq. (1) describes views within the range of sizes it was fitted on, with the effect of resolution absorbed into γ\gamma, and the prediction falls short where the parts reveal objects too small to see in the parent, as above 160 objects (Section 3.2).

Proof of Proposition 1.

Let pk=nk/np_{k}=n_{k}/n be the share of the objects in part kk, so that 0≤pk≤10\leq p_{k}\leq 1 and ∑kpk=1\sum_{k}p_{k}=1. Let J={k:nk>0}J=\{k:n_{k}>0\} be the set of non-empty parts and L=K−mL=K-m its size. Since n≥1n\geq 1, L≥1L\geq 1.

The sum. By linearity of expectation, the expected sum of the parts’ answers is ∑k=1Kc⁡(nk)\sum_{k=1}^{K}c(n_{k}). A part in JJ contributes a​nkγ=a​nγ​pkγ=c⁡(n)​pkγa\,n_{k}^{\gamma}=a\,n^{\gamma}p_{k}^{\gamma}=c(n)\,p_{k}^{\gamma}, and each of the mm empty parts contributes c⁡(0)=sc(0)=s. Hence

∑k=1Kc⁡(nk)=c⁡(n)​∑k∈Jpkγ+m​s.\sum_{k=1}^{K}c(n_{k})\;=\;c(n)\sum_{k\in J}p_{k}^{\gamma}\;+\;m\,s.

An empty part has pkγ=0p_{k}^{\gamma}=0 because γ>0\gamma>0, so the sum over JJ equals A=∑k=1KpkγA=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{\gamma}, and the display is Eq. (2).

The lower bound. For 0<p≤10<p\leq 1 we have pγ=p⋅pγ−1≥pp^{\gamma}=p\cdot p^{\gamma-1}\geq p, because p≤1p\leq 1 and γ−1≤0\gamma-1\leq 0 give pγ−1≥1p^{\gamma-1}\geq 1. Summing over JJ yields A≥∑k∈Jpk=1A\geq\sum_{k\in J}p_{k}=1. If γ<1\gamma<1, the inequality pγ≥pp^{\gamma}\geq p is strict for every p<1p<1, so A=1A=1 requires pk=1p_{k}=1 for each k∈Jk\in J. As the shares sum to one, JJ then has a single member, and all objects lie in one part. If γ=1\gamma=1, every split gives A=1A=1.

The upper bound. The function x↦xγx\mapsto x^{\gamma} is concave on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Jensen’s inequality over the LL non-empty shares gives

1L​∑k∈Jpkγ≤(1L​∑k∈Jpk)γ=L−γ,\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k\in J}p_{k}^{\gamma}\;\leq\;\Big(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k\in J}p_{k}\Big)^{\gamma}\;=\;L^{-\gamma},

hence A≤L1−γ≤K1−γA\leq L^{1-\gamma}\leq K^{1-\gamma}, where the last step uses L≤KL\leq K and 1−γ≥01-\gamma\geq 0. If γ<1\gamma<1, the function is strictly concave, so the first inequality is an equality only if every non-empty share equals 1/L1/L, and the second only if L=KL=K. The upper bound is then reached only when no part is empty and every part holds n/Kn/K objects. If γ=1\gamma=1, both bounds equal one. ∎

The lower bound is the subadditivity of x↦xγx\mapsto x^{\gamma} invoked in the main text. The recursion splits a window into K=4K=4 parts, or into K=2K=2 when the window is elongated (Algorithm 1). With the exponent of Qwen3-VL-8B, 0.76, one split can therefore raise a compressed answer by a factor of at most 40.24≈1.394^{0.24}\approx 1.39, or 20.24≈1.182^{0.24}\approx 1.18. The bound requires an even spread of the objects and no empty part. The medians predicted for this model, which use the true counts of the parts, lie between 1.16 and 1.33 on its two sets of crops. Supplementary Section S1 lists them, tests the model split by split and shows where its assumption fails, in particular for objects too small to be seen in a large view.

Appendix S1 Validation and limits of the response model

Split-level test

We replay the recursion of the horizon measurement from the recorded answers. Every view it looked at, root crop or sub-window, is scored against the annotated objects whose centres it contains. The replay covers 479 of the 480 crops of the first set of DOTA crops and 458 of the second (Section 3.1; Section S2.1). Nineteen crops of the second set coincide with crops of the first and are left out, as are four crops whose windows are not available, one of the first set and three of the second. For the other models the replay covers 458 to 479 crops, the rest having an unanswered or unrecorded view in their tree. The replayed total differs from the original count in 10 of the 479 crops of the first set, which raises the recursive error at three to five objects from +0.08+0.08 (Table S5) to +0.19+0.19 (Table S2) and changes no other bin by more than 0.02. At each split we compare the ratio of the parts’ summed answers to the parent’s answer with AA computed from the true counts of the parts. The exponent is fitted on the unsplit crops of the same model, by least squares of log⁡c\log c on log⁡N\log N over the crops with more than five objects and a non-zero answer.

Table S1 lists the medians per bin of the parent’s true count. For Qwen3-VL-8B the observed and predicted medians differ by at most 0.08 in the five bins from 6 to 160 objects on the first set. Eq. (1) and Proposition 1 were formulated after the replay of the first set, so the second set tests them with every parameter taken from the first. On the second set, with the exponent fixed at 0.76 from the first, they differ by at most 0.10 in four of these bins and by 0.17 at 41 to 80 objects. The second set shares 63 of its 130 images with the first. Restricted to its 249 replayed crops on the 67 images that the first set does not use, the fitted exponent is again 0.76. Observed and predicted medians then differ by at most 0.06 from 6 to 40 objects, but by 0.27 at 41 to 80 and 0.14 at 81 to 160 objects, where the root crops of this subset are answered with 94% and 85% of their objects at the median. For the seven other models the ratio of observed to predicted amplification lies between 0.8 and 1.2 in 35 of their 42 bins above five objects, and between 0.72 and 1.32 in all of them. Parents with at most five objects are split only when they are overcounted. For them the median ratio of the parts’ sum to the parent’s answer is 1.12 on the first set and 1.00 on the second, whereas an exact count would need 0.30 on both. Splitting a view with few objects thus keeps or adds to an overcount.

Error decomposition of the recursive count

Let the recursion on a crop with NN objects end in leaves ℓ\ell that hold nℓn_{\ell} objects and are answered with CℓC_{\ell}. Every object belongs to the leaf that contains its centre, so ∑ℓnℓ=N\sum_{\ell}n_{\ell}=N, and the count is T=∑ℓCℓT=\sum_{\ell}C_{\ell}. Grouping the leaves by their true count gives the identity

T−N=∑ℓ:nℓ>h(Cℓ−nℓ)+∑ℓ: 1≤nℓ≤h(Cℓ−nℓ)+∑ℓ:nℓ=0Cℓ.T-N\;=\;\sum_{\ell:\,n_{\ell}>h}\left(C_{\ell}-n_{\ell}\right)\;+\sum_{\ell:\,1\leq n_{\ell}\leq h}\left(C_{\ell}-n_{\ell}\right)\;+\sum_{\ell:\,n_{\ell}=0}C_{\ell}. (S1)

If the leaves were fixed in advance, Eq. (1) would give the three sums the expectations ∑nℓ>h(a​nℓγ−nℓ)\sum_{n_{\ell}>h}(a\,n_{\ell}^{\gamma}-n_{\ell}), ∑1≤nℓ≤h(a​nℓγ−nℓ)\sum_{1\leq n_{\ell}\leq h}(a\,n_{\ell}^{\gamma}-n_{\ell}) and m0​sm_{0}\,s, where m0m_{0} is the number of empty leaves. The first is the undercount left in leaves that still hold more than hh objects. The second is small, since c⁡(n)≈nc(n)\approx n near the horizon, and the third is the spurious count. In the recursion the leaves depend on the answers. A leaf with more than hh objects that stopped because its answer fell within the horizon was selected for a low answer, so it falls short by more than the undercount alone.

Table S2 gives the three sums, divided by NN and averaged per bin, for Qwen3-VL-8B with h=5h=5. From 11 objects on, the shortfall that remains after subdivision comes from the leaves beyond the horizon, which contribute −0.16-0.16 to −0.24-0.24 per bin on the first set. Leaves with at most five objects hold 9% of all objects on the first set and 8% on the second, so about nine in ten objects end in leaves that still hold more than five. Of the 1,134 leaves beyond the horizon on the first set, 885 could not be split further, at the depth limit or below twice the minimum cell, and 249 had been answered with at most five objects. The empty leaves add a surplus that depends on the scenes, +0.47+0.47 for crops with 6 to 10 objects on the first set but +0.05+0.05 on the second. Leaves within the horizon contribute between −0.07-0.07 and +0.15+0.15 per bin on the first set. On the second set, crops with three to five objects are seldom split, and their single views already fall short by 0.27. Subdivision removes most of the bias, while the spread of the error changes little. Above 20 objects the standard deviation of the recursive error stays close to that of a single view, 14.5 against 16.6 objects at 21 to 40 and 316.0 against 324.0 above 160.

Limits of the model

Eq. (1) gives every view the same response, but the spurious answer and visibility depart from it.

The spurious answer ss is not a single constant. On the first set, sub-windows without the queried class are answered with 2.80 trucks, 1.63 cars, 0.50 storage tanks and 0.21 ships on average. On the second set the values are 2.00, 1.50, 0.67 and 0.09. Views with one to three objects, most of them sub-windows, are answered with 0.71 to 1.08 objects too many. The 120 root crops with one to five objects have a mean error of 0.00 objects. Eq. (1) has no term for this difference between sub-windows and whole crops.

Eq. (1) also assumes that the model can see every object in the view. Above 160 objects the observed amplification of one split is 2.11 on the first set and 2.14 on the second, against 1.33 and 1.32 predicted (Table S1). A fifth of the views with more than 160 objects are answered with at most five, against 6.5% of all views with 11 or more objects. Table S3 shows how often a view beyond the horizon is split. Views with 6 to 10 objects are often answered with at most five and left unsplit, but their answers are nearly unbiased. Beyond ten objects the views left unsplit are mostly answered with zero, and the rule for zero answers splits those that are downsampled. Of the 75 views with more than ten objects that remain unsplit, 51 are answered with zero although they are shown at full resolution.

Zero answers are frequent in large crops. Among the crops with more than five objects, 30 of the 56 crops of 4,096 pixels are answered with zero, against 9 of the 147 crops of 256 pixels. Such answers cannot enter the fit of aa and γ\gamma, which is made on logarithms. On the first set they are 62 of the 359 replayed crops with more than five objects. At a given number of objects, the error of a single view also grows with the side of the crop (Section S2.2). Fitted within one crop side over both sets, the exponent of Qwen3-VL-8B lies between 0.84 and 0.99 for crops of 256 to 2,048 pixels. Larger crops hold more objects in our sample, and crops of 2,048 pixels fall shorter than crops of 256 pixels in every bin. The exponents fitted over all crops, 0.76 and 0.81, are therefore lower than within any of these sides, and they absorb part of the loss of visibility. Visibility enters Eq. (S1) in two ways. A view whose objects are too small to be seen may be answered within the horizon and left unsplit, so that its shortfall falls into the first sum.
