When such a view is split, its parts reveal objects, and their answers exceed the parent’s by more than AA. A part is never shown at a smaller scale than its parent, because it covers less area under the same pixel budget and is enlarged to at least 768 pixels. The VisDrone crops with reduced detail separate this effect from the undercount of crowded views (Section S2.4). Splitting a downsampled view that is answered with zero (Section 4.4) handles the views in which downsampling hides every object.

Fixed grids

Subdivision splits a view only when its count exceeds the horizon. To separate this trigger from splitting as such, we counted every node of the full split tree of each crop, split as the executor splits down to the 256-pixel cell, with Qwen3-VL-8B on the 937 crops of both sets (33,329 views) and with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the 479 crops of the first. Every strategy is then replayed on the same answers. Fixed strategies split every view to a given depth, from 2×\times2 parts down to the 256-pixel cell, or into tiles of at most 1,024 or 512 pixels. Subdivision splits as in Section 4.4, with thresholds hh from 1 to 20, with and without splitting zeros from downsampled views. The cost is the number of VLM calls per crop, including the views that subdivision splits. With greedy decoding, the 9,162 views of Qwen3-VL-8B and 3,956 of Qwen2.5-VL-7B that the horizon measurement also counted receive the same answers as there.

Table S4 gives the results, and Fig. 6 plots those of Qwen3-VL-8B. For this model, subdivision at h=5h=5 and the 4×\times4 grid need 9.4 and 9.0 calls per crop, and over all crops neither is significantly more accurate. By a paired bootstrap over images, subdivision has a median error higher by 0.02 [−0.01-0.01, 0.07] and 1.5 [−1.4-1.4, 4.2] points fewer counts within 20%. Above 20 objects the grid is better, by 0.04 [0.00, 0.06] in median error and 4.3 [1.3, 7.4] points within 20%, the grid taking 10.8 calls per crop against 16.0. With at most 20 objects the grid overcounts by 85% on average, against 1% for subdivision, a difference of 0.84 [0.63, 1.08]. Measured in time on one RTX 3090, the grid takes 2.9 seconds per crop and subdivision 3.8, since subdivision first views the whole crop. Splitting zeros from downsampled views as well, as GeoScope does, subdivision needs 10.4 calls per crop and reaches the grid’s median error of 0.33. On the 249 crops from images that the first set does not use, subdivision and the grid both reach 0.33 in median error, with 36.5% and 36.9% of the counts within 20%. For Qwen2.5-VL-7B the comparison over all crops is again not significant, 0.45 against 0.43 in median error and 28% against 26% within 20%. Its fixed grids overcount sparse crops more, a 4×\times4 grid answering 5.5 times the truth for one or two objects and a grid of 256-pixel cells 14 times. Its subdivision also falls short above 20 objects, by 32% on average, since this model undercounts even small views (Section S2.2). The threshold matters little for either model. From h=3h=3 to h=8h=8 Qwen3-VL-8B needs 10.1 to 9.0 calls per crop and its median error changes by 0.04, since 95% of the splits at h=5h=5 on the first set follow an answer above eight.

Appendix S2 Details and controls of the counting-horizon measurement

S2.1 Crops, exclusions and fitted responses

Images

The crops come from the training part of DOTA-v1.5 (Xia et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2022), whose annotations give every instance as a quadrilateral. We use four classes and ask for them by everyday names. Small vehicles are asked for as cars and large vehicles as trucks, while ships and storage tanks keep their names. The true count NN of a crop is the number of annotated instances of the queried class whose centre, the mean of the four corners, lies inside the crop. Before sampling we remove every image whose DOTA identifier occurs in a benchmark question file, so no crop image, of either set or of Section S2.3, occurs in XLRS-Bench or MME-RealWorld (Section S4.2). Among the remaining images, those with at least three instances of the four classes form the pool. We keep the 130 with the most instances and 130 drawn at random from the rest with seed 0, so that sparse scenes are covered as well.

Crops

Crops are drawn for each pair of image and class, in an order shuffled with the seed of the set. For every side of 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 pixels that does not exceed the longer side of the image, one instance of the class is picked at random. The crop is placed so that this instance lies between 20% and 80% of the side from its upper left corner in each direction. The crop is then shifted into the image and clipped where the image is narrower than the side. This leaves 44 crops of the first set and 66 of the second non-square. A crop joins the bin of its NN until that bin holds 60 crops, and sampling stops when all eight bins are full. The first set uses seed 0 and the second seed 1. Each holds 480 crops, from 112 and 130 images respectively, with 63 images in common, and 19 crops of the second set coincide with crops of the first. The first set holds 188 crops of cars, 119 of trucks, 111 of ships and 62 of storage tanks, the second 241, 125, 87 and 27. Larger crops hold more objects. Over both sets the median NN is 8 for crops of 256 pixels, 33 for crops of 1,024 pixels and 108 for crops of 4,096 pixels. The replay uses the windows of 479 of the 480 crops of the first set and 477 of the second. InternVL3.5 and LLaVA-OneVision are evaluated on these 479 crops of the first set and have 59 crops above 160 objects. The other Qwen models use all 480 crops of the first set, drawn with the same seed.

Views and answers

The native view scales a crop down to at most 204822048^{2} pixels, so square crops of 4,096 pixels are shown at half resolution. A crop whose longer side is below 768 pixels is enlarged to 768 pixels, so crops of 256 and 512 pixels are shown three and one and a half times enlarged. For the Qwen models the processor’s own size limits are lifted, so that the model receives exactly this image. InternVL3.5 and LLaVA-OneVision resize or tile it with their own processors. The question names the class and asks for a single integer (Section S3.2). Decoding is greedy with at most 12 new tokens. The answer is the first integer in the reply, or else the smallest number word from zero to twelve in it. A reply with neither is unanswered and left out of the mean of its bin. For InternVL3.5 and LLaVA-OneVision we add the default system message of each model’s own chat format, which their transformers chat templates leave out. InternVL3.5-8B leaves 7 of its 479 answers without a number, and the other models answer every crop. InternVL3.5-2B, run in the same way, leaves 124 of 479 crops unanswered and is not reported. The subdivision in Fig. 3b follows Algorithm 1 with h=5h=5, depth limit 5 and minimum cell 256 pixels. If any part of a view is unanswered, the view’s own answer is kept. The rule for zero answers from downsampled views is not applied in these measurements.

Models

Qwen3-VL-2B, 4B and 8B (Bai et al., 2025a), Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b), InternVL3.5-4B and 8B (Wang et al., 2025d) and LLaVA-OneVision-7B (Li et al., 2025a) run locally in bfloat16, the last three from their transformers checkpoints. Qwen3-VL-32B is queried through a commercial API with the same views and question. Only Qwen3-VL-8B is run on the second set.

Per-model curves and fitted responses

Table S5 gives the curves of Fig. 3 for every model, and Table 1 the fitted response. Taking the first bin whose mean error falls below −0.2-0.2 as the onset, five of the eight models undercount from 6 to 10 objects, Qwen3-VL-2B from three to five and both InternVL3.5 models from 41 to 80. On the second set alone, Qwen3-VL-8B falls below this mark at three to five objects, with −0.27-0.27. InternVL3.5-4B and 8B overcount one or two objects by 91% and 127% on average, and subdivision raises their surplus, for the 8B model to +1.07+1.07 at 6 to 10 objects. A quarter of the answers of Qwen3-VL-8B to crops with one or two objects are zero. Its mean error there is close to zero because overcounts offset them. The fit of aa and γ\gamma uses the unsplit crops with more than five objects and a non-zero answer. The spurious answer ss is the mean answer to the replayed views that contain no instance of the queried class. All such views are sub-windows, since every crop holds at least one instance. For Qwen3-VL-32B, queried through an API, aa and γ\gamma are fitted on all its crops in the same way, and its recorded answers are replayed like those of the other models.

S2.2 Native versus resized views

The reduced view renders a crop with at most 102421024^{2} pixels instead of 204822048^{2} and is otherwise identical to the native view. Crops whose longer side is below 768 pixels are enlarged to 768 pixels in both views, and crops of 1,024 pixels fit both budgets, so the two views coincide for crops of 256, 512 and 1,024 pixels. With greedy decoding, all 722 such crops of the two sets receive the same answer in both views. The views differ only for the 238 crops of 2,048 and 4,096 pixels, which the reduced view shows at half the scale of the native view.

Over all crops, the reduced view changes the mean error of a bin by at most 0.07 on the first set and 0.11 on the second (Table S6). On the large crops it lowers the mean error from −0.61-0.61 to −0.72-0.72, and it lowers it in seven of the eight bins. These crops fall short already in the native view, by 0.46 at one or two objects and by 0.71 at three to five. The near agreement of the two views over all crops therefore says little about the role of pixel size.

Table S7 breaks down the native view by the side of the crop. At a given number of objects the error grows with the side. Crops of 256 pixels, shown three times enlarged, stay within ±0.21\pm 0.21 in every bin up to 160 objects. Crops of 2,048 pixels, shown at native resolution, fall short by 0.41 to 0.74 in every bin. Crops of 1,024 and 2,048 pixels are shown at the same scale, and the larger ones fall short more in six of the eight bins. At equal object size the error thus grows with the extent of the view. The reduced view shows that at equal extent it also grows as objects get smaller. In our crops the number of objects grows with the side, so the curves of Fig. 3a and b mix the effect of the number of objects with that of the side (Section S1).

The other Qwen models were also run in the reduced view, on the first set. On its large crops the reduced view lowers the mean error of Qwen3-VL-2B from −0.73-0.73 to −0.83-0.83, of Qwen3-VL-4B from −0.63-0.63 to −0.71-0.71 and of Qwen3-VL-32B from −0.63-0.63 to −0.67-0.67. It raises that of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from −0.80-0.80 to −0.77-0.77. Qwen3-VL-32B gives different answers to 63 of the 360 small crops that the two views show identically.

Table S8 repeats the breakdown by crop side for every model, over the crops with 6 to 40 objects and sides up to 2,048 pixels. Every model falls short more in views of 2,048 pixels than of 256 pixels, InternVL3.5-8B by 0.07 and the others by 0.27 to 0.59. Qwen3-VL-8B and both InternVL3.5 models stay within 5% in the smallest views, while the other models fall short by 14 to 33% even there.

S2.3 Prompting variants for counting

We test two alternatives to the direct question that might count more exactly, on a separate set of 240 crops with at most 20 objects. It holds 60 crops in each of the four bins up to 20 objects, drawn by the procedure of Section S2.1 from 87 images, and all three conditions see the same crops in the native view. The enumerate-first prompt asks Qwen3-VL-8B to list every instance with its approximate position, one per line, and to write the total on the last line as ‘Total: N’. It may generate up to 512 tokens, and the answer is the last total, or else the last integer. Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking receives the direct question and may generate up to 2,048 tokens. Its answer is read from the text after its reasoning.

Table S9 gives the share of exact answers and the mean signed error. Neither alternative is significantly more exact than the direct question. Over the 240 crops, the Thinking model answers 4.6 points more crops exactly, with a paired 95% bootstrap interval of [−0.4,+10.0][-0.4,+10.0], and enumerate-first 1.3 points, [−4.6,+7.1][-4.6,+7.1]. Enumerate-first and the Thinking model undercount more at 11 to 20 objects, by 0.59 and 0.49 against 0.16 for the direct question. Enumerate-first leaves 24 crops without a usable number, and the Thinking model takes about ten times as long as the direct question.

Visual programs often count by enumeration, as the length of a list of detected objects (Surís et al., 2023). We compare this with asking for a count on the first set, using 30 crops per bin drawn at random with seed 0. Enumeration asks for a box around every instance of the class, in the grounding format of GeoScope. We allow up to 4,096 new tokens, which hold about 125 boxes, against 1,024 in GeoScope, and drop every box that overlaps an earlier one with an IoU above 0.7. The four conditions are a count in one view, enumeration in one view, the count-triggered subdivision with h=5h=5, and enumeration in every leaf of that subdivision. Table S10 gives the results.

In one view, enumeration degenerates into long lists. Its output reaches the token limit for 17% of the crops with three to five objects and for 57% to 73% of the crops with more than 40. At three to five objects, a fifth of the lists hold more than three times as many boxes as there are objects, up to 128, so the mean error of enumeration there is +4.45+4.45. On the leaves, where every view is small, enumeration is still worse than counting. Above five objects its median absolute relative error is 0.58 to 0.77, against 0.23 to 0.54 for counts on the same leaves. GeoScope therefore asks for an integer in every leaf.

S2.4 Drone imagery

VisDrone2019-DET (Zhu et al., 2022) holds drone images of Chinese cities. Its vehicles are larger in pixels than those of our DOTA crops, with a median size of 30 against 18 pixels. We ask for cars, which merge the cars and vans of VisDrone as DOTA’s small vehicles do, and for trucks. Of the images with at least three such vehicles we take the 150 densest and 150 at random, with seed 0. Crops are drawn as on DOTA with sides of 256 to 2,048 pixels, except that a crop touching an annotated ignore region is discarded, since vehicles there are not annotated. No crop of 2,048 pixels remained, and the bins above 40 objects could not be filled. The 373 crops, 287 of cars and 86 of trucks, come from 179 images. The bins up to 40 objects hold 60 crops each, the bin of 41 to 80 holds 41 and that of 81 to 160 holds 32. Qwen3-VL-8B answers the same question in the native view, with and without subdivision at h=5h=5. To reduce the detail per object, each image is downsampled by a factor and upsampled back to its size with bicubic interpolation before the crops are cut. Windows and views stay the same. A factor of 1.66 brings the median vehicle size to that of the DOTA crops, and a factor of 3 is a stronger test. Table S11 also gives the DOTA crops of cars and trucks with the same sides, 256 to 1,024 pixels, from both sets.

At full detail the single view falls short by at most 0.06 up to 20 objects, by 0.14 at 21 to 40 and by 0.23 at 81 to 160. Undercounts rise from 17% of the answers at one or two objects to 69% at 81 to 160. Round numbers are absent up to five objects and make up 22% of the answers at 6 to 10 and 81% at 81 to 160. Against the DOTA vehicle crops of the same sides, the single view falls short less from 6 to 40 objects, by 0.03 to 0.14 against 0.13 to 0.35. It falls short more at 41 to 80 objects, 0.20 against 0.04, and about as much at 81 to 160, 0.23 against 0.29. Subdivision brings every bin within ±0.09\pm 0.09 and lowers the share of round answers to at most 22%.

Less detail moves the shortfall to fewer objects and deepens it. At three to five objects the single view falls short by 0.01 at full detail and by 0.09 and 0.11 at factors of 1.66 and 3. At 81 to 160 objects it falls short by 0.23, 0.25 and 0.45. Round answers do not follow the detail. At every level they make up about a fifth of the answers at 6 to 10 objects and 81% to 97% at 81 to 160. Subdivision removes the shortfall at a factor of 1.66, leaving errors within ±0.03\pm 0.03 from 6 to 80 objects. At a factor of 3 it leaves −0.08-0.08 to −0.30-0.30 from 6 to 160 objects, and crops with three to five objects, which are not split, already fall short by 0.11. Subdivision thus removes the shortfall at full detail and at a factor of 1.66, and part of it at a factor of 3. A factor of 1.66 moves the shortfall only a little towards fewer objects. From 6 to 40 objects the single view then falls short by 0.07 to 0.19, against 0.13 to 0.35 for the DOTA vehicle crops of the same sides. Object size alone therefore does not explain the later onset of the shortfall on drone images.

S2.5 FAIR1M and DIOR

From the public part of FAIR1M (Sun et al., 2022) we use the 1,732 annotated images, from DIOR (Li et al., 2020) the 11,725 images of its training and validation archive. From each we take 300 images with at least three target objects, half the densest and half at random. On FAIR1M the crops are centred on cars, trucks and ships of every type. Its cars are the small cars and vans, and its trucks the cargo trucks, dump trucks and truck tractors. On DIOR they are centred on vehicles, ships and storage tanks. Bins, the question and the model are those of the DOTA measurement, and subdivision uses h=5h=5. Crops of 256 to 2,048 pixels that fit in the image are drawn as on DOTA, and the whole image is added as one more crop. The images are small, mostly 1,000 pixels on a side on FAIR1M and 800 on DIOR, so the crops are 256 to 1,024 pixels wide or whole images of 800 to 1,500 pixels. Pooled over classes, the model falls short on FAIR1M by 38 to 59% in every bin from three objects on except 41 to 80, and on DIOR it overcounts small sets and is close to unbiased up to 160 objects. Table S12 gives the error per class. This breakdown and the checks below were made after the pooled results were seen. We looked at 16 random crops of each dataset with the annotated objects marked. Most FAIR1M truck annotations are small vehicles that look like cars from above, in crops where the model, asked for trucks, answers zero or one. On DIOR, vehicle crops near marinas appear to be answered with the number of boats, and some crops of coarse images are too blurred for the object to be seen. A few FAIR1M and DIOR crops also hold visible objects of the queried class that are not annotated. For cars on FAIR1M and ships on DIOR, whose names match their appearance, the errors follow the pattern described in Section 3.1, with a later onset than on DOTA.

S2.6 Detectors and fixed grids on FAIR1M and DIOR

A remote sensing system could also count by detecting the objects and counting the boxes. We ran three open-vocabulary detectors on every crop of the horizon measurement: the second DOTA set (458 crops), FAIR1M (480) and DIOR (445), and the first DOTA set (479) to choose their thresholds. The detectors are MM-Grounding-DINO-L (Zhao et al., 2024), whose released checkpoint was trained on Objects365, OpenImages and GoldG according to its model card, OWLv2-L (Minderer et al., 2023) and LLMDet-L (Fu et al., 2025). None of them was trained on DOTA, FAIR1M or DIOR. Each crop is queried with the class phrase the VLM is asked about, in overlapping tiles of 400 pixels (25% overlap) enlarged to 800, the setting that did best for counting on our development questions. Boxes are merged across tiles by non-maximum suppression and a containment test, and the score threshold of each detector, from 0.10 to 0.50 in steps of 0.05, is chosen once on the first DOTA set by the median absolute relative error. The VLM strategies are replayed as in Section S1 on the answers for every part of every crop, which we counted for FAIR1M and DIOR as for DOTA (3,877 views, 0 unparsed). Counting models trained on counting data, such as CountGD and CountGD++ (Amini-Naieni et al., 2024; Amini-Naieni and Zisserman, 2026), are not part of this comparison.

Table 2 gives the results. With the chosen thresholds (0.15 for MM-Grounding-DINO and OWLv2, 0.20 for LLMDet) every detector is less accurate than subdivision as GeoScope uses it on the second DOTA set and on FAIR1M cars. By a paired bootstrap over images, the median error of subdivision is lower by 0.39 to 0.54 on DOTA and 0.34 to 0.55 on FAIR1M cars, and 17 to 23 and 24 to 40 points more of its counts lie within 20% of the truth. The detectors overcount views with few objects. At one to five objects on DOTA they answer 4.1 to 9.9 times the truth on average. In views with more than 160 objects the two Grounding-DINO-based detectors miss about half or more of them on every set, OWLv2 only on DIOR. Chosen on each set itself, the best threshold still leaves the best detector at 0.63 on DOTA and 0.33 on FAIR1M cars, against 0.33 and 0.24 for subdivision. On DIOR ships, in images of 800 pixels, OWLv2 is level with subdivision in median error, 0.14 against 0.11 (paired difference −0.02-0.02 [−0.06-0.06, 0.01]), but its total error is more than twice as large, 0.38 against 0.16 of the true count, because it misses most ships in the densest crops. Over all classes the detectors also do worse in median error, OWLv2 with 0.25 on DIOR against 0.17 for subdivision and MM-Grounding-DINO, the best detector there, with 0.70 on FAIR1M against 0.42.

Fig. S1 shows four crops of the second DOTA set, one per range of true counts, each the crop of at least 1,024 pixels whose error under subdivision is closest to the median of its range. On the three denser crops one view answers 10, while the grid and subdivision come within 11 to 46% of the truth. The detector overcounts all four crops, and the grid overcounts the sparse one sevenfold.

The FAIR1M and DIOR crops also repeat the fixed-grid comparison of Section S1 outside DOTA. Their images are small, so a 4×\times4 grid usually stops at the 256-pixel cell after one split. On FAIR1M cars and DIOR ships it costs 3.2 and 3.0 calls per crop, against 3.9 and 3.6 for subdivision, and the two are equally accurate, 0.24 and 0.11 in median error. Over all FAIR1M classes, which include the trucks whose annotations do not match the question, the grid’s median error is lower, 0.33 against 0.42.

Appendix S3 Implementation details of GeoScope

S3.1 Program grammar

The synthesiser writes one JSON object with two fields. The checker and the executor read only its field program, and the field answer_type is ignored. The checker accepts the programs of the grammar below. Braces, colons and quoted keys are JSON syntax, and the members of an object may appear in any order. Square brackets mark optional members and vertical bars separate alternatives.

Besides the structure, the checker requires one to eight words in the class phrase of every detect, a non-empty expression in every refer and a nesting depth of at most eight below the top operator. It ignores members that the grammar does not name. For UHR-Micro the checker also accepts the region {"op": "box", "box": [x0, y0, x1, y1]}, a pixel box taken from the question (Section S6.9).

The two synthesis prompts offer different parts of the grammar (Section S3.2). The counting prompt, used for RC, XLRS-Bench overall counting and MME-RealWorld counting, offers count and direction with every set and region operator except refer. The relation prompt, used for OSR, offers only direction between two refer nodes. All 80 RC test programs count a class phrase inside the red circle. Programs of type position and color come from a third prompt, written for the position and colour questions of MME-RealWorld. GeoScope leaves these questions to the VLM (Section 7.2). Questions that state a pixel box are not synthesised (Section 4.5).

Table S13 lists how the executor evaluates each operator. A count is evaluated in one of two ways. If its set is a detect of a class cc, an in_region of such a set within a region RR, or a filter or near of one of these two, the VLM counts cc in a window by Algorithm 1. The window is the whole image, the bounding box of RR, or a square of side 2​ρ2\rho at the anchor, cut to the box of RR if there is one. The square is centred on the anchor for near and for the direction CENTER, and otherwise its centre lies ρ\rho away from the centre of the anchor in direction dd. A window other than the whole image is enlarged by 15% of its size on each side if no side exceeds the cell size, 7,000 pixels for MME-RealWorld and 2,000 for XLRS-Bench overall counting. A larger window, the whole image included, is cut into equal cells of at most that size, which are counted separately and summed. For RC the window is the bounding box of the drawn circle enlarged by 15%, counted in one view at 1 M pixels with a question about the objects inside the red circle. Any other set is grounded, and the count is the number of its boxes (Section S3.3).

The mapping from question phrases to operators is not hard-coded. The synthesiser follows the rules and worked examples of the prompts, summarised in Table S14. Before the check, direction words that are not among the nine tokens are mapped onto them. TL, TR, BL and BR, and corner names such as UPPER_LEFT or BOTTOM LEFT, become the corner tokens. UPPER, ABOVE, UP and NORTH become TOP; LOWER, BELOW, DOWN and SOUTH become BOTTOM; WEST and EAST become LEFT and RIGHT; and MIDDLE, CENTRE and MID become CENTER.

S3.2 Prompts and the coverage check

Each prompt is sent to Qwen3-4B as one user turn, with the question in place of <<QUESTION>>. The model decodes greedily with thinking disabled and at most 512 new tokens, and the first complete JSON object of its reply is parsed. Neither prompt contains the answer options. We reproduce both prompts word for word. Line breaks were added to fit the page, so a line that starts with spaces continues the line above, and runs of spaces that align columns are shortened.

The counting prompt holds ten worked examples, six about counting and four about directions, and we print the second, fourth and fifth. The first, third and sixth ask for the airplanes in the entire image, the patches of farmland within a red-circled area and the green cars below a long white building in the bottom left area. The last four ask the first four questions of the relation prompt, written with the operators of the counting prompt.

The relation prompt holds six worked examples, and we print the third and the fourth. The first two ask for the round white storage tank relative to the rectangular pier and for the largest orange warehouse relative to the two baseball fields. The fifth asks for the small blue greenhouse in the lower right corner relative to the cluster of factory buildings. The sixth asks for the white yacht in the marina on the left side of the image relative to the long wooden jetty.

The coverage check compares a counting program with the words of its question and never reads the options. It looks for the words and phrases of Table S15, ignoring case. In the reported configuration it runs on MME-RealWorld counting only. A program that misses any of these words, or that the checker rejects, is synthesised once more, with one of two notes appended to the question on a line of its own:

The first note lists the words that the first program missed. The second program replaces the first if it is well typed and either the first was ill typed or it misses fewer words. RC and OSR programs are executed as first written, and an ill-typed one is answered zero-shot.

The executor asks the VLM four kinds of question. Each view is a crop of the original image, reduced to the pixel budget BB if it is larger. A small crop is enlarged, by at most four times, until its longer side has 768 pixels. Both sides are rounded to multiples of 32 pixels, and the model receives exactly this image. Qwen3-VL decodes greedily, without a system turn. The count question replaces <where> by inside the red circle for RC and by in this image otherwise. Its reply, at most 12 tokens, is read as the first integer it contains, or else as the smallest number word from zero to twelve that it contains. The class phrase is inserted as the program writes it, usually in the singular.

The two grounding questions ask for boxes, the first for a class phrase and the second for a referring expression, with the boxes labelled by its class phrase. A plural expression is asked for as Locate all of …, with bounding boxes. Each reply is cut at 1,024 tokens, about 30 boxes. The boxes are read in the 0 to 1,000 frame of the view, and their order in the reply serves as their score. The fourth kind is the multiple-choice question itself, asked with the views of a pixel box (Section S6.1) and answered by the first-token scores of the option letters.

S3.3 Fallback steps and RC re-counting

Execution degrades in steps, following the fallback design of GeoSelect (Jiang et al., 2026b). Table S16 lists every step of the reported configuration with its trigger and the number of test questions in which it fired.

Synthesis

A repair step rewrites common slips of the synthesiser, by fixed rules that keep the meaning, before the program is checked. Direction words are mapped onto the nine tokens (Section S3.1), and a filter anchored on the image itself becomes in_region with the matching part. A filter whose predicate names proximity, such as NEAR, NEXT_TO, BESIDE or ALONG, becomes near, and one whose predicate is no direction at all is removed. An argmax or argmin with an unknown key becomes top1, and a set given as a region becomes around that set. On the test splits, repair changed 3 OSR and 92 counting programs, each of which the checker would otherwise have rejected. In 43 of the counting programs it turned a proximity predicate into near. For MME-RealWorld counting the checker then rejected 13 programs and the coverage check flagged 458, and each of these questions was synthesised once more. The second program replaced 4 of the rejected programs and 93 of the flagged ones, 58 of which then missed no word. Of the other flagged programs, 350 were kept because the second program missed as many words or more, and 15 because it was ill typed. The missing words were place nouns in 257 of the 458 questions, positions in 255, colour words in 49 and shape words in 40.

Grounding

A class phrase is grounded coarse to fine when the pixel budget shrinks the sides of its window to 60% of their native length or less. The first four boxes of the reduced view are grounded again in close-ups of at least 1,024 pixels and three times their size. A box that its close-up does not confirm is dropped, unless every box would be, and if the reduced view yields no box at all, the window is searched in tiles of about 3,000 pixels. A referring expression that yields no box is replaced by its class phrase, which happened for 122 of the 793 OSR referents grounded on the test split, in 108 questions. If a place container is not found, or the referent is not found in the window around it, the referent is searched for in the whole image with the place phrase appended to its expression. On OSR this happened in 10 test questions. In the OSR configuration an image-part container is always handled this way, because image parts are visible in the whole-image view.

Relaxation

If an anchor or place of a counting program is not found, it is searched for again without its colour and shape words, and then also without its own spatial constraints. Relaxation was tried for 55 anchors and places in 54 counting questions. Ten were found without their colour and shape words, 41 more without their constraints as well, and 4 not at all, so that 50 of the questions could be executed. In 3 more questions an anchor or place was not found and had nothing to drop. On the development split, removing the coverage check and relaxation together lowered counting accuracy from 43.3 to 42.4 and raised the share of abstentions from 2.4 to 6.1%.

Counting

When the set of a counting program is a detect, optionally inside an in_region and that optionally inside a filter or near, the executor turns it into a class phrase and one window, which Algorithm 1 counts. Of the 962 counting programs executed on the test split, 911 had such a set, and for 474 of these at least one view was split. The other 51, of which 43 nest a filter or near inside an in_region, are grounded, and the count is the number of boxes. Coarse-to-fine grounding keeps at most four boxes of a reduced view. The 51 counts lie between zero and four, and 10 of their answers are correct. An unparseable count in a sub-window leaves the count of its parent view in place, and an unparseable count of a whole window abstains, which did not happen on the test split.

RC

The drawn circle is found in a copy of the image reduced to 2,500 pixels on its longer side. Pixels with a red value above 150, green and blue values below 90 and red exceeding both by more than 90 are kept. An ellipse is fitted to the largest connected group of them, preferring groups that fill less than 60% of their bounding box, as a ring does. The circle was not found in 3 of the 80 RC test images, and GeoScope abstained on these questions. A count that equals no option value is taken twice more. The first extra view shows the bounding box of the circle enlarged by 30% on each side, and the second shows the original window enlarged, by at most four times, until its longer side has 1,536 pixels. The median of the three counts is used. Re-counting uses the values of the options, never their order or letters, and the VLM never sees them. It fired for 24 of the 77 executed RC questions. It changed the count in two of them and the chosen option in one, which was wrong before and after, so RC accuracy is the same without it.

Abstention

When every step fails, GeoScope abstains and returns the answer of the zero-shot VLM at 4 M pixels (Section 5.2). On OSR it abstained on 14 questions because a referent was not found, 3 because both referents were grounded on the same box, which leaves no direction, and 1 because its program was ill typed. On MME-RealWorld counting, 9 programs remained ill typed, 7 anchors or places were not found, and 3 regions were empty. Two of them were relative regions less than 8 pixels wide inside the region containing them, and one did not overlap the region containing it. The zero-shot answers are correct for 1 of the 3 RC, 3 of the 18 OSR and 8 of the 19 counting questions on which it abstained. With LLaVA-OV-7B as the perception model, GeoScope abstains on 182 of the 400 OSR test questions, mostly because one of the two referents is not found.

S3.4 Program correctness and coverage

We wrote reference programs by hand for 150 questions, 30 test questions per task and 30 development questions each for OSR and MME-RealWorld counting. For each we judged whether the synthesised program expresses every constraint of the question, without looking at the answer. All 30 RC programs are acceptable, as are 34 of the 60 OSR programs and 27 of the 60 counting programs. Most faults are simplifications. Of the 33 faulty counting programs, 16 drop the place and keep the image part, so that the parking lot in the lower right becomes the lower right, and 10 write a relation the question does not state. OSR programs most often attach a scene condition to only one of the two objects, in 9 cases, or add a direction the question does not name, in 7. Questions with acceptable and unacceptable programs are answered correctly at similar rates, 41% and 42% for counting and 44% and 38% for OSR. Replacing the synthesised programs by the hand-written ones on the test questions changes accuracy by at most two of thirty per task, from 19, 11 and 11 correct answers to 19, 13 and 11 for RC, OSR and counting.

Of the 245 development counting questions, 43 use constructions the grammar lacks, mostly words for the state or action of an object, ordinals and between. Their simplified programs are answered correctly in 51.2% of the cases, against 41.6% for the other questions.

S3.5 Prompt sensitivity and choice of synthesiser

Prompt variants

We changed each synthesis prompt in two ways and ran the development split with the rest of the configuration unchanged. The first variant removes the guidance, which is the RULES block of the counting prompt and the four lines that explain the fields of a referring expression in the relation prompt. The second keeps every other worked example, five of ten and three of six. Table S17 gives the results. RC programs did not change at all. For OSR and counting, 33 to 61% of the programs stayed identical, and two of the four variants were significantly less accurate: OSR with every other example by 10.0 points and counting without the guidance by 6.1. The guidance of the counting prompt and the examples of the relation prompt are thus needed, and the programs depend on the wording of the prompt.

Choice of synthesiser

Table S18 replaces Qwen3-4B by five other synthesisers and keeps everything else, the prompts included. Two are vision–language models, Qwen3-VL-4B and the perception model Qwen3-VL-8B, each given the question alone or the question and the image at 4 M pixels. The other three are text models from other families, the dense transformers Phi-4-mini (Abouelenin et al., 2025) and Llama-3.2-3B, a smaller model of the Llama 3 family (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and the state-space model Falcon3-Mamba-7B, a continued pre-training of Falcon Mamba 7B (Zuo et al., 2024). An ill-typed program goes through the same fallback steps as in GeoScope (Section S3.3). No synthesiser does better than Qwen3-4B. The vision–language models lose 4 to 7 points on OSR, none significantly on 100 questions, and 3.7 to 5.7 points on counting. The loss on counting is significant for Qwen3-VL-8B, with differences of −5.7-5.7 [−10.6-10.6, −0.8-0.8] points without the image and −5.3-5.3 [−10.2-10.2, −0.8-0.8] with it. Showing the image changes accuracy by +0.4+0.4 to +3.0+3.0 points, and none of the four paired intervals excludes zero, the largest gain being +3.0+3.0 [−1.0-1.0, +8.0+8.0] on OSR for Qwen3-VL-8B. The image raises the share of well-typed programs of Qwen3-VL-4B from 79 to 89% on OSR and from 86 to 93% on counting. Without the image, 74 of the 245 counting programs of Qwen3-VL-8B are ill typed. Phi-4-mini writes well-typed programs for 98, 91 and 100% of the OSR, counting and RC questions, Llama-3.2-3B for 57, 56 and 20%, and Falcon3-Mamba-7B for 77, 94 and 5%. On RC, whose programs are simple, every synthesiser reaches the 60.0 of Qwen3-4B except these two, which fall to 45.0 and 40.0. With Qwen3-VL-4B as the perception model, letting it also write the programs lowers OSR from 50.0 to 40.0 and counting from 35.5 to 33.5, and leaves RC at 45.0. Among Qwen3 text models of 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and 8B parameters, the 4B model writes the best programs, with 47, 49, 56 and 46 on OSR and 38.4, 41.6, 43.3 and 40.8 on counting. The prompt variants and the five synthesisers were evaluated after the configuration had been frozen, and they did not change it.

Appendix S4 Evaluation protocol

S4.1 Splits

Each task is split once by a fixed rule, and the split is stored with its questions. The question identifiers of the task are sorted and shuffled with Python’s random.Random, seeded with the string 0- followed by the task name, for instance 0-OSR. The first 20% of the shuffled identifiers, rounded to the nearest integer, form the development split, and the remaining 80% the held-out test split. RC is thus split into 20 development and 80 test questions, OSR into 100 and 400, and MME-RealWorld counting into 245 and 981. The same rule splits the 13 other tasks we evaluate, from 12 and 48 questions for the smallest XLRS-Bench subtasks to 251 and 1,006 for MME-RealWorld position. Applying the rule to the stored question files reproduces the stored split of all 16 tasks. Every RC and MME-RealWorld counting question has its own image, so these splits share no image. Of the 400 OSR test questions, 32 use an image that a development question also uses. Without them GeoScope scores 44.02 against 34.51 for zero-shot answering, and resampling images instead of questions gives the gain of 10.5 points an interval of [4.3, 16.7], against [4.2, 16.8]. The splits of RC, OSR, XLRS-Bench overall counting and MME-RealWorld counting were drawn before the first experiment.

Every configuration was fixed before it was run on a test split.

S4.2 Leakage checks

The crops of the counting horizon (Section 3.1) come from DOTA-v1.5 training images (Xia et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2022), a source that XLRS-Bench and MME-RealWorld also draw on. When the images were chosen, every DOTA image named in the benchmark question files then in use was left out. After the measurement we compared the images of both DOTA crop sets with the 1,220 DOTA images named in all 3,080 XLRS-Bench and 3,738 MME-RealWorld remote sensing questions, and found none in common. FAIR1M, DIOR and VisDrone, the other sources of horizon crops (Section S2.5 and Section S2.4), are used by neither benchmark. The image paths of the two benchmarks name only DOTA, MiniFrance, HRSCD, Potsdam, ITCVD and Toronto.

The two synthesis prompts hold 16 worked examples. Four questions appear in both, so the examples ask 12 distinct questions. We compared each example with the 4,398 questions of RC, OSR, XLRS-Bench overall counting and MME-RealWorld counting, position and colour, of both splits, by the similarity ratio of Python’s difflib on lower-cased letters and digits. No example equals a benchmark question. Four have a ratio above 0.85, all because they follow a benchmark sentence pattern with other objects. The other ratios are at most 0.80. The closest pair, at 0.96, is the example How many white trucks are there in the upper left corner of the picture? and the test question How many white cars are there in the upper left corner of the picture?

The guidance lines of the prompts quote short phrases as illustrations. Most of them, such as near the river or the cluster of houses, occur in questions of both splits. Two occur in test questions only, L-shaped black roof building in OSR question 75 and below the yellow buildings in OSR question 272. We had read both questions in a random sample of all questions that we drew to describe the data. GeoScope answers both wrongly, and without them its OSR test accuracy is 44.22 instead of 44.00.

S4.3 Zero-shot protocol

Our zero-shot reference for Qwen3-VL-8B is well above the MME-RealWorld numbers that other papers report for the same model, 56.41 on position, 48.07 on colour and 21.35 on counting (Ma et al., 2026b), values that Zhang et al. (2026c) also reports and Jiang et al. (2026a) reports to one decimal. To see where the difference comes from, we answered the development split with five protocols (Table S19). The first is ours, the image at 4 M pixels and the option letter chosen by the logit of the first answer token. The second keeps input and prompt but generates an answer of up to 64 tokens and parses the letter from it. The third is ours at 1 M pixels. The last two use the prompt and answer extraction of MME-RealWorld’s official evaluation, copied from VLMEvalKit, at 4 M and at 1 M pixels.

The input size accounts for most of the difference. Going from 4 M to 1 M pixels costs 11.2 points on position, 10.8 on colour and 9.4 on counting. The way of answering matters much less. At 4 M pixels a generated answer or the official prompt and extraction move the three MME-RealWorld tasks by at most 2.9 points. With the official protocol at 1 M pixels we obtain 61.75, 56.97 and 19.59, within 9 points of the reported numbers. On RC and OSR, whose development splits hold 20 and 100 questions, the protocols differ by amounts that such small sets cannot resolve.

S4.4 Constant-answer baseline

The constant-answer baseline answers every question of a task with the same option position, a letter, or the same option-value rank, such as the largest number, whichever is most often correct on the development split. On RC the smallest number and letter A tie there with 8 of 20 correct, on OSR letters A and C with 30 of 100, and on XLRS-Bench overall counting letters B, C and D and the largest and second-largest numbers with 4 of 12. We break such ties by the test score, so the baseline is an upper bound for the tied choices; breaking them by the first option letter instead gives 26.25 on RC and 22.50 on OSR.

Appendix S5 Reproduced methods

S5.1 Selection of methods

For each task we reproduce, with its official code, the training-free method with the strongest result reported on that task by early October 2026. We count a method as training-free if none of its components was trained by its authors, while frozen models trained by others are allowed. Table S20 lists the results behind the choice.

On RC the strongest result is WeaveEarth’s 47.0, measured by RS-OPSD (Jiang et al., 2026a), since WeaveEarth itself reports RC only merged with overall counting into one category. On OSR and on XLRS-Bench as a whole the strongest results are GazeEarth’s 37.8 and 53.51, the latter by question. On MME-RealWorld counting, the table of ZoomSearch (Zhou et al., 2025) lists 40.25 for RAP and 39.15 for ZoomSearch, both with LLaVA-OneVision-7B, and we reproduce both. RAP reports no remote sensing results itself (Wang et al., 2025e). Its code supports Qwen3-VL-8B, so we also run it with GeoScope’s backbone. WeaveEarth, GazeEarth and ZoomSearch report MME-RealWorld position and colour as well, and we run them on these two tasks too (Section S6.2).

The lower block of Table S20 lists the methods we do not reproduce. ZoomEye (Shen et al., 2025), RADAR (Liu et al., 2026d) and ImageRAG (Zhang et al., 2025c) report counting results below those of RAP and ZoomSearch, and the results ImageRAG reports for itself use an answering model fine-tuned by its authors. DualComp (Li et al., 2026b) and SA-GEM (Ma et al., 2026a) compress or prune visual tokens under a router trained offline by their authors. They fall outside the training-free track, although SA-GEM’s 41.6 would otherwise be the strongest result on OSR. Concurrent work without public code is not reproduced, and trained methods enter the comparison through their published numbers (Table 6). The exception is Text-Before-Vision (Wang et al., 2026a), the only published method that reports a higher XLRS-Bench average than GeoScope. We re-run it with its released checkpoint (Section S5.5).

S5.2 Settings of the reproduced methods

Table S21 summarises the runs. Each training-free method runs its released inference code, with the changes described below for each method, on the test questions of the listed tasks, with greedy decoding and its own answer extraction. Our wrappers load the questions, write one record per question and, where needed, move models between GPU and host memory. Each of these runs used one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 with 24 GiB, the GPU of our own experiments. The re-run of the trained Text-Before-Vision is described in Section S5.5. Methods built on Qwen3-VL-8B load the same copy of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct as GeoScope. ZoomSearch and RAP load the original LLaVA-OneVision-7B checkpoint through their own code, while our zero-shot and GeoScope runs with this model use its transformers release with the model’s default system message. An answer from which a method’s extraction recovers no option letter counts as wrong.

WeaveEarth

We import its only inference script, written for open-ended questions, with all its default settings. The script has no multiple-choice template, so its question slot receives the question, the lettered options and the instruction to answer with the option’s letter, the same text that RAP receives. Its prompt also names the question category, which we set to the benchmark’s own task label, such as regional counting or count. For MME-RealWorld position and colour we use position and color. The released requirements pin a transformers version that cannot load Qwen3-VL, so we use version 4.57.1. The SigLIP2 encoder that scores the tiles truncates its text at 64 tokens, which cuts the options and the instruction from 319 of the 400 OSR and 870 of the 981 counting queries, and we left this unchanged. Peak memory stays below 21.4 GiB, so no change was needed to fit the GPU.

GazeEarth

We use its released configurations for MME-RealWorld and XLRS-Bench, which agree in every setting of the method. The frozen model selects at most two cells of a 4×44\times 4 grid on a 1,536-pixel overview and answers from a foveated 2,048-pixel view. Its answer prompt asks for the reasoning before the answer, within 1,024 generated tokens, and its own matcher scores the answer. Of its 981 counting answers, 68 were cut off at this limit before giving an answer. Questions that state a pixel box skip the selection call. GazeEarth resamples the original pixels, so it always receives the original image. For the eight XLRS-Bench subtasks outside counting and spatial relations, it receives the original images of the XLRS-Bench-lite release. Two changes were needed for the code to run. The overall land-use questions have several correct letters, which we pass to the scorer as a separated list because it rejects a string such as BCD. An exception inside the pipeline is recorded and its question recomputed, where the released runner would stop.

ZoomSearch

We use LLaVA-OneVision-7B (Li et al., 2025a) answering and VisRAG-Ret (Yu et al., 2025) scoring patches, the configuration its repository recommends. Paper and code disagree on two parameters of the search. Tables 6 and 7 of the paper set the depth bias bb to 0.3 and, for LLaVA-OneVision, the minimal search unit uminu_{\min} to 448 pixels on images of at least 4,000 pixels and to 112 on smaller ones. The released code fixes uminu_{\min} at 224 and bb at 0.2 for every image. We run both settings, each with the code’s 10 search steps and its other values. The paper setting applies to all RC questions and to 398 of the 400 OSR and 925 of the 981 counting questions, while the smaller images keep the code values. With umin=448u_{\min}=448 the released splitting rule ends the search at regions of about 1,100 pixels on a 10,000-pixel image, against about 370 pixels with 224.

The released evaluation script reads the options from a column that the repository’s MME-RealWorld loader does not provide, and the evaluation files behind the paper are not public. We append the options in the format of the repository’s demonstration files and extract the answer with its MME-RealWorld evaluation code. LLaVA-OneVision-7B in half precision, VisRAG-Ret and their activations do not fit together in 24 GiB. Unchanged, the official code runs out of memory at the root of every search, catches the error and answers without searching. Our wrapper therefore keeps only the model about to run on the GPU and the other in pinned host memory, with weights, precision and computation unchanged. Swapping adds 3.8 to 4.6 s per question with the paper’s settings on the tasks of Table 4 and up to 7.5 s in the other runs, and this time is included in all times we report. No question in the reported runs ends in an error caught by the official code. With the code defaults ZoomSearch answers 42.50% of the RC, 31.75% of the OSR and 29.97% of the counting questions correctly, against 42.50, 32.50 and 31.50% with the paper’s settings. It also needs 1.5 to 2.2 times as long per question, 211, 182 and 96 s against 96, 86 and 62 s. The paper’s settings are therefore the ones in Table 4.

RAP

We use VisRAG-Ret as retriever and the code’s default bias of 0.2. With Qwen3-VL-8B we take the 10 search steps of the repository’s script for that model, with crops of 224 pixels, or 336 pixels when the long side exceeds 5,096. With LLaVA-OneVision-7B we take the 200 steps of the repository’s only script for that family, written for its 0.5B model, with crops of 112 pixels, or 448 pixels when the long side is at least 4,000. RAP has no configuration for MME-RealWorld, so it receives the multiple-choice text we give WeaveEarth and the answer extraction we use for ZoomSearch. Its two models alternate on the GPU as in ZoomSearch, which adds 1.9 s per question. With Qwen3-VL-8B, the forward pass that scores a layout by the model’s confidence reads only the logits of the last position, and we compute only that position. The score is unchanged up to rounding, while the full pass runs out of memory at 16,384 visual tokens. Of the 981 answers with Qwen3-VL-8B, 65 contain no option letter.

RAP takes 400 s per question with Qwen3-VL-8B and 828 s with LLaVA-OneVision-7B, 90% and 98% of it in confidence passes. With LLaVA-OneVision-7B it was therefore run on a fixed 20% subset of the counting test split, the 197 questions at positions 1, 6, 11 and so on when ordered by identifier. With Qwen3-VL-8B it was run on the whole split. This subset is GeoScope’s weakest, at 29.95 against 34.18 to 40.31 on the other four. On it, RAP reaches 35.53 with either model, 8.1 points [2.0, 14.2] above zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B and 5.6 [−0.5-0.5, 11.7] above zero-shot LLaVA-OneVision-7B. On the whole split, RAP with Qwen3-VL-8B gains 5.2 [2.3, 8.1] over zero-shot Qwen3-VL-8B (Table 4).

S5.3 Reported and reproduced numbers

Table S22 lists, for every task on which a method reports a number or another paper re-ran it, the numbers each reproduced method reports for itself, our reproduction, and the re-runs published by other papers. We count a number in another paper as a re-run only if that paper states that it ran the method, reports a run time it measured for the method, or reports the method on a benchmark on which the method itself reports nothing. Numbers equal to the method’s own are copies and are left out. The table thus draws on four papers. GazeEarth (Zhang et al., 2026c) states that every number it does not mark as taken from the original paper was reproduced with the official code and parameter configurations, and its ZoomSearch rows carry no such mark. WeaveEarth (Ma et al., 2026b) reports for ZoomSearch an inference time of 54.25 s per sample over its two benchmarks, which differs from the 53.94 s that ZoomSearch reports for itself. RS-OPSD (Jiang et al., 2026a) reports per-sample inference times for ZoomSearch and WeaveEarth and per-subtask XLRS-Bench numbers that neither method reports; its MME-RealWorld numbers for both repeat their own, for WeaveEarth with the three categories in permuted columns, and are left out. GeoVista (Zhu et al., 2026) describes the settings in which it ran its baselines on XLRS-Bench, where ZoomSearch reports nothing. RS-OPSD runs ZoomSearch with LLaVA-OneVision-7B, as we do; WeaveEarth and GazeEarth describe the model behind their ZoomSearch runs only as 7B and 8B, and GeoVista does not name it.

Every re-run by another paper is below the number the method reports for itself, and in each such case our reproduction lies between the two. Counting with ZoomSearch shows the spread, with 39.15 reported, 31.50 in our runs, and 20.05 and 17.86 in two later papers. On RC and OSR, where ZoomSearch reports nothing, our numbers are within 0.5 points of those measured by RS-OPSD, whose authors include all four authors of ZoomSearch. On XLRS-Bench overall counting, which Table 4 leaves out, RS-OPSD measures ZoomSearch at 46.7 on all 60 questions and we measure 37.50 on the 48 test questions, its only re-run well above ours. In our runs WeaveEarth exceeds its reported MME-RealWorld numbers by 2.8 to 7.2 points, and GazeEarth its counting number by 6.0 points.

On XLRS-Bench, GazeEarth answers 976 of the 2,464 held-out questions correctly, 39.61%, and reports 53.51% on all questions. Its backbone answers 46.71% zero-shot. GazeEarth falls below the backbone on seven of the 13 subtasks. It falls most on object classification and object colour, 35.31 and 31.56 against 48.44 and 43.44 on 1,280 questions together, and on counting with change detection, 20.83 against 43.75. It is above the backbone on five, most on route planning and environmental condition reasoning, by 8.8 and 7.5 points.

S5.4 Gains against each method’s own baselines

GazeEarth’s code contains two baselines with the same backbone and answer prompt: an overview, which answers from the whole image reduced to 2,048 pixels on the long side, and direct answering from the native image through the backbone’s processor. We ran the overview on six tasks, the three of Table 4, overall counting and MME-RealWorld position and colour. We ran direct answering on MME-RealWorld position, where GazeEarth reports a gain of 14.7 points over it, second only to its 15.6 on colour (Table S23).

Against its own overview, GazeEarth gains 6.6 points on colour and loses 2.7 on position, in line with the +8.1+8.1 and −1.3-1.3 its paper reports for these two tasks. On the other four tasks the differences are not significant. Direct answering, which its paper reports at 56.41 on position with the same backbone, reaches 71.67 in our run of its own code, 4.6 points above GazeEarth and 3.0 [0.4, 5.7] below our zero-shot reference. Our zero-shot reference is stronger than the reported ones mainly because the image is given at a larger size (Section S4.3).

S5.5 Text-Before-Vision

Text-Before-Vision (Wang et al., 2026a) fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-7B and then trains it with reinforcement learning to zoom into the image with a crop tool. It reports 60.40 on XLRS-Bench, the mean accuracy of 32 sampled answers per question, without results per subtask. We ran its released checkpoint with its released evaluation code on all 3,080 questions as prepared by its own data script. We ran it in its two modes: greedy, with up to 1,024 tokens per turn, and sampled, with one answer per question at temperature 0.7 and up to 10,240 tokens per turn, which estimates its Pass@1 without bias. In both, the model may call the crop tool at every turn, for at most eleven turns in the greedy script and ten in the sampled one. For safety, the checkpoint shards are read without running pickled code and the tool calls are parsed as literals instead of being evaluated; neither change alters the computation. The model is served with vLLM on two NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs with tensor parallelism of two, as in its script, and with its full context of 128,000 tokens. We disabled video input, which the evaluation never sends, and reserved 80% of the GPU memory.

The two rules differ in how they read a reply (Table S24). Ours takes one answer per question, as for every method: the letter in the answer tag or, if the tag is missing, the last “Answer: X” of the reply. Text-Before-Vision’s own scoring code takes every standalone letter of the reply, the article “a” included, and counts a single-choice answer as correct when any of them is the answer. With greedy decoding only 544 of the 3,080 replies close the answer tag. The other 2,536 end with a line “Answer: X” instead, and for each of them its code re-sends the same request up to ten times. Over the greedy replies its scoring gives 59.54, close to the 60.40 it reports, and ours 50.54. With sampling every reply closes the tag, and both rules give 47.47. One sample per question estimates the Pass@1 that the paper reports, with a standard error of at most 1.3 points, so the 12.9 points between 47.47 and the reported 60.40 are not sampling noise. The model calls the crop tool 50 times in the greedy run and 107 times in the sampled one, over 3,080 questions each.

On the held-out 80%, where Text-Before-Vision scores 50.54 greedy and 48.15 sampled under our rule, GeoScope’s 59.53 is 9.0 points [5.8, 12.2] and 11.4 [8.0, 14.7] higher in the mean over subtasks. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the model Text-Before-Vision is trained from, GeoScope reaches 56.93 on the held-out questions, 8.0 [5.9, 9.9] above that model’s zero-shot answers. It is 6.4 [3.5, 9.4] and 8.8 [5.5, 12.0] points above Text-Before-Vision’s greedy and sampled answers. Against GeoScope with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on all questions (Table S24), its greedy answers are about 20 points better on overall land use and route planning, two subtasks GeoScope leaves to its backbone, worse on overall and regional counting, spatial relations and the three subtasks about the object in a given box, and at most five points apart on the rest.

Appendix S6 Additional results

S6.1 XLRS-Bench by subtask

Table S25 lists the 13 subtasks of XLRS-Bench-lite on all 3,080 questions and on the held-out 80%, 2,464 questions. Three routes answer them. Typed programs answer RC, OSR and overall counting. The three object-property subtasks give the target as a pixel box and are answered from a close-up around it (Section 4.5). Qwen3-VL-8B answers the other seven subtasks zero-shot, so GeoScope’s accuracy there equals the zero-shot column.

The zero-shot protocol is that of Section 5.2 with two adjustments, both fixed before the test questions were run. The change-detection questions give the model both images of the pair. The 100 overall land-use questions, 97 of which have several correct options, are answered by generating letters and scored by exact match of the letter set, the rule of GazeEarth’s scorer.

The pixel-box route renders a close-up centred on the box, three times its longer side and at least 512 pixels wide. It outlines the box in red and shows the whole image, also outlined, as a first view. The rendering was chosen among three on the 332 development questions of the three subtasks. The close-up alone reached 74.10, the outlined close-up 85.24 and the outlined close-up with the whole image 86.75, against 39.16 for zero-shot answering.

Averaged over the 13 subtasks, GeoScope reaches 59.98 on all questions and 59.53 on the held-out questions, against 48.83 and 48.57 for zero-shot answering. By question it reaches 71.82 and 71.51, against 45.65 and 46.71. On all questions, the highest published training-free result is GazeEarth’s 53.51 by question (Zhang et al., 2026c), and the trained GeoLens and GeoEyes report 54.2 and ScaleEarth 59.4, on a split it does not state, as means over subtasks (Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a). The trained Text-Before-Vision reports 60.40 from sampled answers, against 47.47 when we re-run its sampling (Section S5.5).

Table S26 regroups the subtasks into the eight categories of GazeEarth’s table. Under this grouping each of its published category accuracies corresponds to a whole number of correct answers. GeoScope is above GazeEarth on counting, spatial relations and object properties, which GeoScope answers by programs and pixel boxes. It is below GazeEarth on the five categories it leaves to its backbone. Object properties hold 1,660 of the 3,080 questions and account for 22.8 of GeoScope’s 26.2-point gain by question over zero-shot answering.

S6.2 MME-RealWorld position and colour

GeoScope leaves the position and colour questions of MME-RealWorld to its backbone (Section 7.2). On the development split we tried programs that ground the object and then read its position from geometry or name its colour on a close-up. They reached 74.9 for position against 73.7 zero-shot, a difference of 1.2 [−4.4-4.4, 6.8], and 60.6 for colour against 65.7, a difference of −5.2-5.2 [−12.0-12.0, 1.6]. Answering the original question from the whole image together with a close-up of the grounded object reached 54.2 on position and 67.7 on colour. Neither program gains clearly on the development split, so both tasks go to the frozen VLM.

Table S27 lists the test split. GeoScope’s answers are those of Qwen3-VL-8B zero-shot, 74.65 on position and 63.55 on colour. None of the three reproduced methods that report these tasks significantly improves on the zero-shot answers of its own backbone. WeaveEarth falls significantly below them on both tasks, by 5.4 and 5.0 points, and GazeEarth by 7.6 points on position, while its 0.5 on colour is not significant. ZoomSearch changes the 62.62 and 58.47 of LLaVA-OneVision-7B by −1.7-1.7 [−5.4-5.4, 1.9] and 1.3 [−2.3-2.3, 4.9], neither significant. Question by question, GeoScope is 13.7 points [10.0, 17.4] above ZoomSearch on position and 3.8 [0.1, 7.5] on colour, both owed to its backbone. On all questions the backbone reaches 74.46 and 63.98. Together with GeoScope’s 37.93 on counting they give the MME-RealWorld average of 58.79 in Table 6, or 58.96 weighted by questions. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B the backbone reaches 67.94 and 49.96, and the average with GeoScope’s 34.18 on counting is 50.69.

S6.3 Answer options of MME-RealWorld counting

Each MME-RealWorld counting question offers four numbers and a fifth option stating that the image does not show the number. The fifth option is correct for 5 of the 1,226 questions, all in our test split. The four numbers are listed in ascending order in 449 of the 981 test questions, in descending order in 106 and in mixed order in 426. Where the correct number sits among them depends on the count (Table S28). For one or two objects it is never the largest number offered, and for 6 to 10 objects it is the largest in 52% of the questions.

For the restricted answers of Section 7.1, our zero-shot protocol scores the option letters by the logit of the first answer token (Section S4.3), and the restricted answer is the numeric option with the highest of these logits, from the same forward pass. Table S29 lists both answers for every model we ran zero-shot. Qwen3-VL-32B returns letters without scores, so its answers cannot be restricted to the numeric options. ZoomSearch, run on LLaVA-OV-7B, is 4.0 points [0.3, 7.7] below the restricted answers of Qwen3-VL-8B on the test split.

GeoScope’s counts run high for 11 to 20 objects, which the layout above rewards, and how much depends on the backbone. We take the test questions answered by an executed count. With Qwen3-VL-8B the median ratio of GeoScope’s count to the truth is 1.00 for up to five objects, 1.25 for 6 to 10, 1.94 for 11 to 20 and 1.29 above 20. With LLaVA-OneVision-7B it is 1.00 for one or two objects, 0.67 for 3 to 10, 1.83 for 11 to 20 and 1.32 above 20. LLaVA-OneVision-7B returns a box covering at least 80% of its search window for 14% of its groundings, against 6% for Qwen3-VL-8B, so its programs restrict the region less.

S6.4 Results by image source

The counting horizon was measured on DOTA crops (Section 3.1), and 96% of the MME-RealWorld counting images come from DOTA. Most RC and OSR images do not. Of the test questions, 59 of the 80 RC and 271 of the 400 OSR use images from MiniFrance, HRSCD and ITCVD. Table S30 breaks down the test questions by image source.

With Qwen3-VL-8B the gains on non-DOTA images are 20.3 points [5.1, 35.6] on RC and 9.2 [1.8, 16.6] on OSR, against 4.8 and 13.2 on DOTA images. On RC the gain comes from MiniFrance, 33.3 points on 36 questions. On the 22 HRSCD questions the interval of every backbone includes zero. With LLaVA-OneVision-7B the RC gain is positive on every source and significant on DOTA and MiniFrance images. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B the OSR gain is confined to DOTA images, 15.5 [6.2, 24.8] against −1.8-1.8 [−8.5-8.5, 4.8] elsewhere. The 44 MME-RealWorld counting questions from Potsdam and Toronto are too few to show an effect, −6.8-6.8 [−25.0-25.0, 11.4] with Qwen3-VL-8B.

S6.5 Test-split ablations by true count

Table S31 gives the counting ablations of Table 8 on the test split, by the true number of objects NN. We recompute each region count from the VLM answers recorded in the test runs, under three rules. The final rule accepts a count within the horizon unless it is a zero from a downsampled view. A second rule also accepts such zeros, and a third, without subdivision, counts once every view that the program first renders. Under the final rule every recomputed count and answer equals the original, and every rule uses only recorded answers. Questions answered by the fallback keep their answer under every rule. The same option matching maps each count to an option, and the intervals come from a paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples.

With programs and Qwen3-VL-8B, neither of the other two rules has a significant effect, overall or in any stratum. When the whole image is counted, as in the run without programs, the trade-off of Proposition 1 appears. Removing subdivision then costs 4.6 points [0.4, 8.8] on the 261 questions with 6 to 20 objects and gains 2.1 [−0.1-0.1, 4.4] on the 700 with at most five. Accepting such zeros costs 3.8 and gains 2.4 on the same questions. Within the regions that programs name, the losses on 6 to 20 objects shrink to 2.7 points for subdivision and 1.9 for accepting such zeros, neither significant. Qwen3-VL-4B undercounts more strongly, with an exponent of 0.64 against 0.76 on DOTA crops. Removing subdivision costs it 2.2 points [0.6, 4.0] overall and 5.4 [1.1, 9.6] on 6 to 20 objects. Only 15 test questions ask for more than twenty objects, and Qwen3-VL-8B loses two of them without subdivision, with or without programs. On OSR, replacing the direction-relation matrix by the centre angle on the same boxes changes accuracy by −2.0-2.0 [−5.5-5.5, 1.5] with Qwen3-VL-8B and −1.8-1.8 [−4.5-4.5, 1.0] with Qwen3-VL-4B.

The fixed grid needs new answers. For every question whose program counted one region, we tiled the counted region into the cells of the test run, split each cell into a 4×\times4 grid as the executor splits views, counted every part with the same question, view and pixel budget, and matched the sum to an option as before. Every other question keeps its recorded answer. Subdivision, re-run in the same way on 20 of these questions, reproduced every original count. Over the test split the grid lowers accuracy by 2.9 points [−0.1-0.1, 5.8], with 15.8 VLM calls per counted question against about 14 for subdivision. It picks the largest number offered for 64% of the questions about at most five objects, against 33%, and gains 20.7 points [14.9, 26.6] on the 222 questions whose answer is the largest number offered while losing 9.8 [6.5, 13.1] on the 754 others. By the true number of objects, the grid loses 8.0 points [4.1, 11.7] on the 700 questions with at most five objects and gains 11.5 [6.9, 16.1] on the 261 with 6 to 20 (Table S31). Both changes follow from where the correct number sits among the options. The gain comes mostly from the 128 questions with 6 to 20 objects whose answer is the largest number offered, where it reaches 18.0 points [10.9, 25.8], against 5.3 [0.0, 10.5] on the other 133. For questions about at most five objects the median count of the grid is 2.7 times the truth and 15% of its counts lie within 20% of the truth, against an exact median and 24% for subdivision. On the 48 test questions of XLRS-Bench overall counting the grid needs 172 calls per question, against about 53, and loses 10.4 points [−2.1-2.1, 22.9]. It picks the largest number offered for every question with 1 to 20 objects, and it loses 22.2 points [8.3, 36.1] on the 36 questions whose answer is a smaller one.

S6.6 Direct answers on the program’s window

To separate where a program looks from what it computes there, the backbone answered each test question directly on the window its program chose, with the question and its options and the first-token scores of the option letters. The windows are those recorded in the test runs. On RC the window is the crop that was counted, at 1 M pixels. On OSR it is the union of the boxes of the two referents, enlarged to 1.3 times its longer side and to at least 768 pixels, at 2.5 M pixels. On MME-RealWorld counting it is the counted region with its margin, at 2.5 M pixels; the 51 programs that count grounded boxes have no region and are left out. Only questions whose program executed are compared, with GeoScope’s executed answer before any fallback (Table S32). A direct answer takes one VLM call, against a median of two, five and seven calls for GeoScope on RC, OSR and counting (Section 6.5). On MME-RealWorld the direct answer picks the option stating that the image does not show the number for 31% of the questions, so the table also gives the highest-scoring numeric option.

S6.7 InternVL3.5-8B as the perception model

To see whether GeoScope depends on the Qwen family, we replaced its perception model by InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025d) on the development split. The synthesiser, prompts, parsers and parameters stay as they are, and boxes use the same coordinates from 0 to 1,000. InternVL3.5 receives the default system message of its own chat template. Its zero-shot answers at 4 M pixels, scored by first-token letter logits, serve as reference and fallback. Table S33 gives the results.

With InternVL3.5-8B, GeoScope gains 13.1 points [6.1, 19.6] on counting, and its accuracy is not significantly different from that of GeoScope with Qwen3-VL-8B, −2.4-2.4 [−8.6-8.6, 3.7], although GeoScope was tuned on this split with Qwen3-VL-8B. On OSR its gain of 5.0 is not significant, and it abstains on 15 of the 100 questions, 13 of them because no direction could be computed. On counting it abstains on 45 of the 245 questions, 28 of them because the count InternVL3.5 returned could not be parsed. On RC it gains nothing and stays 20 points below GeoScope with Qwen3-VL-8B. RC asks mostly about small sets, with a median of three objects, and on DOTA crops InternVL3.5-8B overcounts one or two objects by 127% on average (Table S5).

S6.8 Sensitivity to pixel budget, horizon and margin

All variants of the pixel budget BB and the horizon hh were run on the development split only (Table S34), and the test runs of OSR and counting use B=2.5B=2.5 M pixels and h=5h=5. On OSR the development accuracy peaks at the chosen budget, 56 against 42 at 1 M and 43 at 4 M pixels. On counting the curve is flatter, with 38.8, 43.3 and 41.2. The held-out OSR accuracy of the chosen budget, 44.00, is close to the development accuracy of the other two budgets, so most of the peak is the noise of choosing among variants on 100 questions. The zero-shot reference is at its best at 4 M pixels or within noise of it, with 45, 23 and 26.5 on RC, OSR and counting against 40, 25 and 19.2 at 2.5 M and 35, 25 and 17.1 at 1 M pixels.

The horizon matters little. On the development counting questions, with the configuration that still accepted zeros from downsampled views, h=3h=3, 5 and 8 give 40.4, 41.2 and 41.2. On the first set of DOTA crops of Section 3.1, the recursive errors for the three values nearly coincide beyond ten objects. The number of views falls only from 4,660 to 4,063 as hh grows from 3 to 8, because most splits are decided by large answers and by the minimum cell rather than by the threshold. A larger hh splits fewer small sets and lowers the surplus at 6 to 10 objects, from 31% at h=3h=3 to 24% at h=8h=8, as Proposition 1 predicts for splits below the horizon. For Qwen3-VL-2B, whose shortfall begins at three to five objects, h=2h=2 reduces the error at 6 to 10 objects from −23-23% to −12-12% but leaves −38-38% at 11 to 20 objects.

When every accepted count must come from a native-resolution view instead of being triggered by the answer, development accuracy falls from 41.2 to 37.1 and the median relative count error rises from 0.71 to 1.00, with more overcounts.

The 15% margin around a counted region was also chosen on the development split. With a margin of 5% or none, development counting accuracy falls from 43.3 to 40.0 and 37.6, the latter by 5.7 points [−9.4-9.4, −2.4-2.4]. Among the questions counted in one view of their region, 80 or 81 counts are too high at every margin, while those too low rise from 50 to 59 and 67 and the exact ones fall from 34 to 25 and 19. A narrower window thus cuts off objects on the border of a coarsely grounded region and does not remove overcounts. Counts of whole images, which have no margin, are the same in all three runs.

S6.9 UHR-Micro data, protocol and breakdown

Data

We use the test split of the five task types in Table 7, 1,369 questions, and the validation split of the same task types, 100 questions each, whose images the test split does not use. The public release lacks 105 of the SODA-A images these questions use. We took them from the SODA-A release (Cheng et al., 2023) by their file number; three images present in both releases are identical pixel by pixel. All questions are evaluated.

Zero-shot answers

The benchmark’s code for direct answering runs on several large GPUs and its output instructions are not released. We re-run Qwen3-VL-8B on one RTX 3090 with its released image preprocessing (up to 16,777,216 pixels), its conversion of pixel coordinates in a question to a 0–1,000 grid, the question followed by its closing instruction, greedy decoding, and its released parser and metric. Every answer is parsed. The re-run lies within 3.4 points of the reported scores on four task types and 7.5 points above on conditional counting (Table 7). InternVL3.5-8B is re-run with its own preprocessing, up to 12 tiles of 448×448448\times 448 pixels and a thumbnail, and otherwise in the same way; it lies within 4.4 points of the reported scores on all five task types. We compare GeoScope with the re-run of its backbone, question by question.

GeoScope

The counting programs run with the frozen configuration of MME-RealWorld counting. Of the 544 regional counting questions, 461 give the region as a pixel box. For them the program counts the class in that box, which needed one addition to the program language, a region given by its corners; the other 83 describe the region in words and are synthesised like every counting question. On the validation split, the usual 15% view margin around a given box scored 48.30 against 45.34 without it on the 84 questions with a box, and was kept. The direction and distance questions mark the reference object in red and the others in blue, green, yellow or purple, each in one fixed colour. The executor takes the bounding box of the largest connected outline of each colour and answers from the boxes, the direction by the direction-relation matrix as for OSR and the distance between box centres. On the validation split these rules agree with the reference answer on all 200 questions, as do the centre angle and the distance between box edges. The configuration was fixed on the validation split before the test split was evaluated. Three regional and 19 conditional counting questions fell back to the zero-shot answer. With InternVL3.5-8B the same frozen configuration runs with that model as the VLM, set up as in Section S6.7, and 2 global, 10 regional and 58 conditional counting questions fall back to its zero-shot answer. For 44 of the 58 the place or anchor that the question names is not found or is grounded with an empty box; the other 14 have programs that are not well typed, as with Qwen3-VL-8B.

Horizon of InternVL3.5-8B

The shortfall of InternVL3.5-8B begins beyond 40 objects (Table 1), and the upper end of the bin before it gives h=40h=40. A larger threshold only removes splits, so the counts with h=40h=40 follow from the answers already recorded with h=5h=5. On the test split, global counting rises from 42.23 to 44.01 (+1.8 [−0.2-0.2, 3.8]), regional counting falls from 58.77 to 56.88 (−1.9-1.9 [−3.2-3.2, −0.5-0.5]) and conditional counting is 26.40 against 26.19 (+0.2 [−1.2-1.2, 1.4]).
