On the validation split the differences are +5.6, −2.7-2.7 and +0.6. The answers that change show why. In global counting, 92 of the 108 changed answers with h=5h=5 are too high, the spurious counts of splits below the horizon; InternVL3.5-8B answers an empty view with 2.4 objects on average, the most of the models in Table 1 (column ss). With h=40h=40 fewer views are split, and on the 83 of these questions about at most 20 objects the score rises. Of the 25 about more objects, 19 answers with h=40h=40 are too low against 5 with h=5h=5, and in regional counting the 164 changed answers about more than 20 objects include 90 that are too low against 76. On these views the single-view answers of InternVL3.5-8B already fall short below 40 objects, as the horizon depends on the view (Section 3.1), and h=40h=40 accepts them where h=5h=5 splits. With h=40h=40 the global count would be the highest in Table 7, above the 43.19 of MAP, and the regional count below its 57.81. Neither threshold is better on both tasks, and the table keeps h=5h=5 for both backbones.

Breakdown by question type

On the test split, GeoScope scores 53.30 against 11.76 on the regional counting questions with a box and 27.36 against 20.72 on those that describe the region. On conditional counting, the 93 questions about a fine-grained aircraft type score 8.3 against 3.3, and the other 109 score 25.3 against 40.6; their median signed relative error is zero, but the counts scatter widely, as for any question whose place is grounded wrongly.

Without subdivision

To measure what subdivision adds, we take the recorded answer of Qwen3-VL-8B on the first, unsplit view of every counted region in the test run, the view a count without subdivision would use. Abstained questions keep the zero-shot answer, and the eight global counting questions whose image is cut into cells keep their full count, which slightly understates the effect. On global counting the full system scores 40.49, the unsplit view alone 24.87 and zero-shot answering 23.71, so subdivision adds 15.6 points [11.7, 19.6], while counting the whole image in one view adds 1.2 [−1.4-1.4, 3.8] over zero-shot answering. On regional counting the three score 49.34, 42.43 and 13.13. Restricting the count to the given box adds 29.3 points [26.3, 32.4] and subdivision 6.9 [4.6, 9.2].

Appendix S7 Cost breakdown

Table S35 lists the mean seconds per question that Fig. 7 plots against accuracy, and also those of RAP with LLaVA-OV-7B on the fixed 20% subset of the counting split, which the figure leaves out.

Table S36 breaks down the cost of GeoScope with Qwen3-VL-8B on 20 RC, 60 OSR and 60 counting questions of the development split. All runs use one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 with 24 GiB from a fresh start, and times exclude model loading. Every VLM call records its answer when it returns. Within a question, the time between consecutive records is charged to the later call, and the time after the last call to execution. Visual tokens count one token per 32×3232\times 32 pixels of every image the VLM receives. Synthesis was timed separately with Qwen3-4B from a fresh start, one question at a time and in batches of 16, the batch size of our runs.

Nearly all of the time goes to VLM calls. Grounding is the expensive kind, at 3.6 to 9 s per call, because the VLM generates a list of boxes, while a count costs about 0.45 s. An OSR question spends 24.3 s on 6.7 grounding calls on average, and a counting question 12.6 s on 1.4 grounding calls and 7.3 s on 16.4 counts. RC needs no grounding, since the red circle is found by its colour, and its crop is counted 2.9 times on average. Executing a program takes less than 10 ms. Counting has a long tail, with a median of 6.7 s and a maximum of 185 s for a region that needs deep subdivision. Peak GPU memory is 19.3 GiB for perception and 14.5 GiB for synthesis.

The same programs were also served with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), on the same GPU and questions, with the independent calls of a question issued concurrently: the parts of a split view, the cells of a long window and the zoom windows of a coarse-to-fine search. The mean time per question was 2.3, 22.2 and 13.6 s for RC, OSR and counting, against 1.8, 24.3 and 19.8 s, and the longest counting question took 67 s instead of 185 s. Served one call at a time, the times were 2.3, 23.3 and 22.9 s. The served model gave a different answer on 8 of the 140 questions, mostly through different grounding outputs, so all reported results use the original implementation.

The reproduced methods were timed on the test questions, on the same GPU model, from their per-question records. WeaveEarth scores tiles with SigLIP2 and calls its VLM once per question, in 5.6 to 6.9 s. GazeEarth makes two calls per counting question, with 5,435 visual tokens and 329 generated tokens on average, in 16.0 s. ZoomSearch scores 20.1 to 24.0 views per question with the confidence of its VLM, and RAP 30.9 layouts with Qwen3-VL-8B and 379.8 with LLaVA-OneVision-7B, whose setting allows 200 steps. For reference, WeaveEarth reports 7.59 s per sample for itself on an NVIDIA A100, averaged over the two benchmarks it evaluates, and ZoomSearch reports 60.02 s per MME-RealWorld remote sensing sample without naming the GPU, against 62.1 s in our runs.

Appendix S8 Failure analysis and examples

Hand-written programs change at most two of thirty answers per task (Section S3.4), so we look at what perception gets wrong on the test split. Of the 209 OSR questions answered wrongly by an executed program, the computed direction lies more than 45 degrees from the correct option in 179, and is roughly opposite to it in 48. With both referents grounded on the right objects, the computed direction would lie near the correct option, so errors this large mean that a referent was grounded on a different object, or that the annotation disagrees with the geometry. Only 30 wrong directions lie within 45 degrees of the correct option, near the boundary between two options. Of the 605 counting questions answered wrongly with a numeric answer, 243 are off by one or two objects and 249 by more than five. The count is too low in 315 and too high in 290.

XLRS-Bench overall counting asks for all instances of a class in the image, mostly ships, cars and boats, which make up 38 of the 48 test questions. The true counts have a median of 61.5 and reach 734. Adjacent options differ by a median of 17% of the smaller one, so a count must lie within about 8% of the truth to select the correct option. GeoScope cuts the image into cells of at most 2,000 pixels and counts each with count-triggered subdivision. Its counts are nearly unbiased, with a median signed error of −0.9-0.9%, 25 too low and 21 too high. Their median absolute error is 17.7%, however, and only 9 of the 48 lie within 8% of the truth. Table S37 compares the methods we ran. GeoScope gains 25.0 points over its zero-shot backbone and is 2.1 points below both ZoomSearch and always choosing the second-largest number, with intervals of about 20 points either way.

Table S38 shows two executions on MME-RealWorld counting test questions, both with a program that counts a class in one quarter of a 4,096-pixel DOTA image. In the first, the lower-left quarter, widened by 15% on each side, is too large for one view at 2.5 M pixels, and the model answers 7. Since 7 exceeds the horizon, the view is split into four parts at native resolution, whose counts of 0, 0, 4 and 5 are accepted and sum to the true 9. The zero-shot model chose 3. In the second, the first view answers 10, and one part again exceeds the horizon. The leaves sum to 11 ships where the annotation has 2, and option matching selects the largest option, 4, while the zero-shot model answers correctly. The recorded answers do not show whether the extra ships are spurious answers or real ships that lie in the quarter but outside the corner the question means. For one or two objects the correct number is never the largest offered (Table S28), so such an overshoot always fails.
